pains.title: Fake or edited payment receipts and unverified QR/bank transfers at the counter
pains.description: Customers show an edited or reused DuitNow/QR/bank-transfer screenshot (or a 1-sen transfer edited to look like the full amount, or a 'request for money' made to look like a payment), take the goods, and leave. The owner or staff only discover the loss later when they check the bank app. It hits stalls, bazaar traders, shops, minimarts and food sellers, and is reported repeatedly across 2024-2025 in Malaysian media from owners' own TikTok/X/Facebook posts. Underlying operational gap: no fast, reliable way for a busy counter to confirm that money actually landed before handing over goods, and no end-of-day match of claimed vs received payments.
pains.who: Micro retailers, pasar malam/Ramadan bazaar stalls, food sellers, small shops and minimarts accepting QR/DuitNow/bank transfer; also B2B suppliers (one police case involved supplier companies).

evidence.what_it_says: Cosmetics shop (TikTok @zilabeautyshop, likely Johor Bahru) says a customer edited a QR payment receipt to avoid paying RM300. Owner: "RM300 mungkin kecil untuk peniaga besar, untuk kami peniaga kecil boleh cover bayar gaji seminggu" and warned the edited font was hard to notice at a glance.

Port Dickson supermarket lost RM780 (six packs of Nescafe, seven packs of Milo) to a couple who showed a fake transfer receipt. Trader: "When we checked the account, there was no credit transaction — just a 'request for money' notification."

evidence.source: SAYS Seismik citing X posts by traders (Malaysia)
evidence.what_it_says: Ramadan bazaar kuih stall: "Jumlah yang masuk tu tak kena dengan kadar jualan. Cuma separuh je yang masuk." A nasi kerabu seller says a customer reused the same payment proof image for a second purchase that was never paid.
Sungai Petani pasar malam: suspect made a one-sen transfer and edited the receipt to buy a RM54 watch; she tried two other watch shops; she said a friend had succeeded with the method several times.

Kunafa business owner (Ojen) alleges RM246,611 lost to a personal shopper using edited receipts over eight months (TikTok post cites 200 fake receipts); RM69,300 repaid so far. Owner: "saya dan staf penat berniaga".
Per search-result summary (page not fetched): Selangor police broke a syndicate using fake payment receipts against supplier companies, solving six cases with losses of RM166,338.10.

pains.frequency: Daily exposure for any counter accepting transfers; multiple publicised incidents per year 2024-2025, one alleged case ran 200 receipts over 8 months. Peaks during Ramadan bazaar season.
pains.money_impact: Per incident RM54-RM780 for retail; RM300 described as a week of staff wages for a small shop; one alleged case RM246,611; supplier syndicate RM166,338.10 across six cases; one bazaar stall received about half of expected QR sales.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Immediate and usually final: goods leave with the customer; recovery depends on CCTV, viral posts or police reports.
pains.already_spending: Staff/owner time checking bank apps per sale; some sellers rely on payment terminals with sound notifications; police reports and social-media naming to recover money. No figure for tool spend found.

pains.title: B2B customers stretch payment terms (30 days becomes 60/90/120) and starve small suppliers of cash
pains.description: Small B2B suppliers and service firms deliver, invoice, then chase. Owners describe customers (including 'big companies') routinely paying far beyond agreed terms, leaving thin margins wiped out and cash tied up while wages, rent and suppliers still fall due. Chasing is manual (calls/WhatsApp). Small firms have weak leverage and fear losing the customer.
pains.who: Small B2B suppliers, contractors, service businesses and small manufacturers selling on credit terms to larger firms.

evidence.source: Lowyat.NET forum thread 'i give up being a business man/entreprenuer'
evidence.what_it_says: OP tyrionlannister99: "most customers like to ask for discounts. then when ask for payments, always got delay. 30days become 60days etc". drug5: "Collecting payment is always an issue. Always 30 days became 60/90/120 days." zstan: "kononnya big company but owe me money for more than 2 months still havent pay."

evidence.source: Lowyat.NET forum thread 'How your business doing?'
evidence.what_it_says: Gentleman_League: "Facing cash flow and creditors delay payment sigh.." Others: "still bleed salary of staff and maintenance fee".

evidence.source: The Star via PressReader (Malaysia), seen as search result only
evidence.what_it_says: Per search-result summary (not fetched): a SME Media Group and INTI International University survey found 73% of business operators called late payment part of Malaysian business culture, with some SMEs waiting up to 94 days. OLD source; no primary copy of the survey found.

evidence.source: Curlec blog 'Manual Payment Collection Problems Hurting Malaysian SMEs' (vendor)
evidence.what_it_says: Vendor blog summarising Experian Malaysia State of Credit 2025 as showing Malaysian SMEs face longer payment delays than larger corporations; no figures given on the page. (A search-result summary attributed 'average delays improved from 64 to 61 days' to Experian 2025; not verified.)

pains.frequency: Every invoice cycle (monthly for most B2B relationships); chasing is weekly or more for overdue accounts.
pains.money_impact: Cash tied up for 60-120 days instead of 30; one owner says payment delay leaves 'no peanuts at all' margin. No Malaysia-specific 2024-2026 ringgit figure found in owner voice.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Owner's own wages, rent and supplier bills still due on time; Limitation Act 1953 gives six years to recover a debt (mishu.my, 2025-02-22); small claims procedure reportedly not usable by companies (Lowyat comment, unverified).
pains.already_spending: Owner/admin time chasing; letters of demand and lawyers in bad cases; some owners switch to COD-only terms to avoid it (MISMan, Lowyat 2021: 'payments were ok, coz i did COD. 30days terms max').

pains.title: Consumer pre-orders and 'pay later' customers: deposits not taken, balances never paid, last-minute cancellations, dine-and-dash
pains.description: Home-based and small food sellers (kuih, cookies, cakes, murtabak, restaurants) lose money when customers order then cancel or vanish, promise to pay the balance later, pay by transfer 'later' and delay for days, or leave without paying. Sellers react by forcing 'booking with payment', but tracking who has paid what, deposits and balances is manual on WhatsApp. Small grocers extend informal credit (hutang) logged in a ledger book and lose it when customers abscond.
pains.who: Home-based F&B sellers, bakeries, bazaar stalls, small restaurants, kedai runcit with credit customers.

evidence.what_it_says: George Town raya cookie sellers report customers cancelling at the last minute or disappearing (excuses like card failure, blocking the seller's number). Sal Bakery: "Jadi saya terpaksa menggunakan konsep 'booking with payment' bagi mengelak kerugian berganda."
Jerantut Ramadan bazaar murtabak stall handed over 50 murtabak (RM400) after a QR payment that never went through; noticed only after breaking fast; recovered after posting in a Facebook group.
Restaurant (owner 'Cikta'): group of ten left RM93 unpaid after saying they would pay at the counter. "Tapi sudah sehari berlalu, tiada siapa yang datang untuk bayar".

evidence.source: theSun (Malaysia), seen as search result only (fetch returned 403)
evidence.what_it_says: Per search-result summary: home-based kuih seller complained on Threads that a customer often failed to pay, chose online transfers then delayed; she chased a RM5 debt for several days; a commenter said the owed total reached nearly RM100 before the seller gave up.
Online sellers list 'Barang dahulu, bayar kemudian': customers receive goods then are "menghilangkan diri serta tidak dapat dihubungi". OLD source.

Owner: "We have 20+ on credit nepali"; "Maximun credit is RM500/ person. after hutang more than RM500 we block the accounts."; "we have some myamar and pakistan not paying us. they run away from their company."; records kept in "just a ledger book and customer signed after buy". OLD single source.

pains.frequency: Weekly for active food sellers; concentrated in festive peaks (Ramadan, Raya, CNY). Grocery credit is daily.
pains.money_impact: Per incident RM5-RM400 in the cited cases, plus wasted perishable stock already produced; grocery credit capped at RM500 per person with absconding debtors.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Perishable goods: once made and uncollected or handed over unpaid, the loss is immediate (spoilage, no resale).
pains.already_spending: Owner time chasing on WhatsApp/Threads/Facebook; switching to full prepayment risks losing customers; ledger books for credit.

pains.title: Cash and sales leakage from staff not recording sales; owners cannot reconcile till, POS and stock
pains.description: Owners find staff taking cash payments without keying them into the POS, or stock going missing, and cannot tell how long it has been happening. Forum replies recommend end-of-day balancing, linking inventory to sales, and CCTV linked to POS, all of which the owner must set up and check manually.
pains.who: Small F&B outlets, cafes, kedai runcit and retail shops with a few staff handling cash.

evidence.source: Lowyat.NET 'Caught my employee stealing' (F&B owner briantwj)
evidence.what_it_says: "I checked my Point of Sales system, no orders were taken for what the customer is eating." "The money involved this time is around RM30+. But I'm not sure how many times this have happened already." Reply (slepth): "You need an end-of-the-day checking. See if everthing are balanced." Reply (Fenix98): "Thief will steal again.. My own experience..."

evidence.source: Lowyat.NET kedai runcit thread, seen via search-result summary
evidence.what_it_says: Per search-result summary (not in fetched portion): a kedai runcit owner reported missing items around 1%, and a commenter warned that skipping stock checks can leave owners losing money to staff. Unverified quote.

pains.frequency: Daily cash handling; owner discovers leakage irregularly.
pains.money_impact: RM30+ per incident in the cited case, unknown cumulative; possible ~1% stock shrinkage (unverified).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: No external deadline; loss accumulates silently until detected.
pains.already_spending: POS systems, CCTV (some linked to POS), owner time on end-of-day checks.

pains.title: Bookkeeping, receipts and tax compliance cost money and owner time; no clerk to do it
pains.description: Micro owners pay accountants monthly, run handwritten bills, and face shifting e-invoice rules. Hiring a clerk is hard and costly, so the owner does paperwork after hours. E-invoicing is now exempt for businesses under RM3 million sales from 1 Sep 2026, but owners already paid for software, and bookkeeping/tax filing remain. Owners in their own words describe time as the biggest issue.
pains.who: Micro and small owners (sole props, one-man Sdn Bhds, workshops, hawkers) without an admin hire.

evidence.source: Lowyat.NET 'My friend will be Retired Early' (about a 61-year-old JB workshop owner)
evidence.what_it_says: "Right now, accounting services are also costing him an extra RM 1,500 per month!"; "he has been using handwritten bills for over 20 years"; "Nowadays, hiring a clerk is difficult"; "No one wants to take an RM2,000 salary and work in Johor Bahru."; "The biggest issue is time." Revenue RM200,000 (2023); e-invoice software about RM300/month per the OP.

acbc asks whether the government expects "one man show companies to sit down and do paperwork?"; vhs: "the rules kept being tweaked since day 1 until now"; upcars: "Lucky I can cancel my e-invoice subscription"; DogeGamingPRO: "Rip those sudah invest in system kek".

syyang85: "it started feeling more like a full-time job, especially with all the accounting terms and processes to manage." "Better to hire an accountant. No way around it." "The more manual work involved, the higher the risk of errors."

Owner: "My 1st business is all over the place in terms of accounting and tax."; "I have to manually make payments and calculate"; needs salary slips, EPF and SOCSO deductions; "Storehub does not have accounting system". OLD.

Government raises e-invoice exemption threshold from RM1mil to RM3mil (per search summary, effective 1 Sep 2026, over 1.1 million businesses exempt). Reduces e-invoice as a micro-SME pain; bookkeeping/tax remain.

pains.frequency: Monthly (accounting, payroll, statutory contributions); daily for receipts/bills.
pains.money_impact: Accountant RM1,500/month for one RM200k-revenue workshop; e-invoice software ~RM300/month (OP estimate); audit RM1,000-3,000/yr for small Sdn Bhd (Lowyat anecdotes 2006-2022, via search summary only).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Tax filing and statutory deadlines; e-invoice fines of RM200 to RM20,000 per breach cited in a news excerpt (search summary only, unverified); one owner considered closing the shop.
pains.already_spending: Yes: outsourced accountants, tax agents, company secretaries, POS/e-invoice subscriptions.

pains.title: Large customers delay or withhold payment from small suppliers over e-invoice paperwork
pains.description: Even after the RM3 million exemption, SME associations report large corporate customers asking exempt suppliers for e-invoice information, and warn of payments being delayed because a small supplier does not issue an LHDN-validated e-invoice. Earlier, big buyers circulated warnings that non-compliant suppliers could be dropped. Combines compliance confusion with cash collection.
pains.who: Exempt micro/small suppliers selling to large companies already on e-invoicing.

evidence.what_it_says: Dr Chin Chee Seong (SME Association of Malaysia) warns of exempt suppliers "or their payments being delayed simply because they are not issuing e-invoices". Datuk William Ng: "larger corporate clients already subject to e-invoice were actively asking some exempt suppliers for information"; "payments should not be withheld simply because an exempt SME could not provide an e-invoice".

DARE survey of 516 micro online sellers: 59.9% had never heard of e-invoicing, 78.1% worried about effect on operations; William Ng said large corporations issued circulars warning non-compliant SME suppliers of exclusion from supply chains.

pains.frequency: Every invoice to an affected large customer (monthly or more).
pains.money_impact: Delayed or withheld payments to small suppliers; no ringgit figure found.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Risk of exclusion from large buyers' supply chains; payment held until paperwork satisfies the buyer.
pains.already_spending: Some SMEs already paid for accounting systems, integration and staff training (Datin Christine Koh, The Star 2026-09-04).

forums.context_notes:
Coverage limits: Reddit is blocked for this agent's search and fetch (API error 400), so no r/malaysia, r/MalaysianPF or r/smallbusiness posts were collected. The shared web-search budget (200 calls across all agents) ran out after about 30 of this agent's searches, so these angles were not searched: Shopee/TikTok seller fees and return/refund abuse, staff no-shows, supplier lateness and stock-outs (2024-2026), Cari/Threads/X. Lowyat.NET worked well as an owner-voice source; Malaysian news outlets (Kosmo, SAYS, The Vibes, The Star) mostly repeat owners' own TikTok/X/Threads posts. Many Lowyat threads are 2019-2023 and are marked OLD. Items labelled 'search-result summary' were seen only in search snippets and were not fetched; check them before citing to judges.

Market context: e-invoicing is now mostly a non-issue for micro firms. The exemption threshold rose from RM1mil to RM3mil, announced 30 Aug 2026 (The Star), and search summaries say it took effect 1 Sep 2026 and covers over 1.1 million businesses. The remaining e-invoice pain is indirect: large buyers pressing exempt suppliers (The Star, 4 Sep 2026). Labour context: owners say hiring a clerk is hard and minimum wage rises have pushed costs up (Lowyat 2023 and 2025), so admin falls on the owner. Lowyat comments also say small claims may not be open to companies (unverified).

Convenience pains that miss the bar: customers asking on WhatsApp at any hour (Kosmo 2022-03-03 reports a 4am cake-order call; SAYS 2017 'bertanya tak kira waktu'), plus Lowyat 2021 complaints about council and bomba inspections. Mystery COD parcel scams (The Star, 1 Aug 2026) hit buyers, not sellers. Not researched here: an Orbyte or Alpha Red Solutions product profile.

Strongest money signals for an idea: (1) checking that a payment actually arrived at the counter or before handover, and matching claimed payments to the bank feed each day (pains 1 and 3); (2) tracking deposits, balances and who owes what, with automatic reminders (pains 2 and 3); (3) end-of-day cash, POS and stock reconciliation (pain 4).

pains.title: Cash stuck in unpaid invoices: SMEs wait about 2 months or more to be paid
pains.description: Micro and small firms deliver goods or services first and wait for payment. Experian puts the average SME payment delay at 64 days in early 2025, against 58 days for large corporations. MAMBA says micro and small firms wait 60 to 120 days. That gap means they cannot pay salaries, suppliers and rent, or restock. Seven in 10 SMEs hold less than six months of cash reserves. In October 2026 a think tank said Budget 2027 still does not address the cash-flow problem, and the SME minister publicly asked for stronger late-payment protection. Malaysia has no late-payment law. Collecting money remains each owner's job.
pains.who: Micro and small B2B suppliers: transport/logistics, wholesale, hospitality, contractors and subcontractors, and suppliers to corporates, GLCs and government. Experian data covers SMEs as a whole, with no micro-only breakdown.

evidence.source: Experian Malaysia, State of Credit 2025 release
evidence.what_it_says: SME payment delays fell from 69 days (2022) to 64 days in early 2025. Large corporations averaged 58 days. In 1Q 2025 the SME-vs-corporate gap was 26 days in transport/logistics, 13 days in hospitality and 10 days in wholesale. Quote: "SMEs in Malaysia could be more vulnerable, with liquidity being a significant challenge compared to larger corporations."

evidence.source: FocusM, quoting MAMBA secretary-general Alvin Low
evidence.what_it_says: The article says micro and small firms "often deliver products and services upfront but only receive payment 60 to 120 days later". Low: "This significant waiting period creates immense strain, making it difficult to cover operational costs like salaries", and to "replenish inventory". He calls factoring "under-utilised" and cites a US$21.5bil (RM90.30bil) MSME funding gap (2024 SME Finance Forum).

evidence.source: The Star, quoting think tank Insap
evidence.what_it_says: Insap says Budget 2027 "still does not address the core problem of cash flow". "The pressing question is whether they can pay suppliers, rent and salaries in the coming months." It cites the SME Association: "seven in 10 SMEs have less than six months of cash reserves". In July 2026 the association warned that micro and small firms "may face critical operational distress within three to six months without liquidity relief".
KUSKOP minister Steven Sim hoped Budget 2027 would bring progress on "strengthening late-payment protection" for SMEs. Bernama reports this indirectly, not as a direct quote.

The DPM criticised unpaid rural-road (JALB) contractors who had already finished their work. He said some contractors had closed and others were sued by material suppliers and subcontractors. He said smaller contractors, suppliers and workers down the chain suffer too, and he ordered a "Zero Pending Operation".
Per the search result, Malaysian law "provides no framework when it comes to late payment". Parties set interest and collection terms by contract. Search snippet only, not fetched.

pains.frequency: Continuous, on every invoice cycle. Average delay is 64 days for SMEs (Experian 2025), or 60-120 days for micro firms per MAMBA.
pains.money_impact: No RM figure for micro firms. Firms cannot cover salaries, suppliers or rent, and some contractors closed (Sept 2026). The MSME funding gap is RM90.30bil (2024, cited by MAMBA). 7 in 10 SMEs have under 6 months of cash.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Payroll, rent and supplier due dates arrive while receivables are still outstanding. Suppliers and subcontractors sue unpaid contractors, and some contractors close (KKDW case, Sept 2026).
pains.already_spending: Factoring and invoice financing (MAMBA calls them under-utilised), bank loans and retained earnings. Owner and staff time spent chasing payments is not quantified in any source found.

pains.title: Fake orders from impersonated government agencies or large customers drain micro sellers
pains.description: A syndicate pattern that repeats across states in 2025-2026. A WhatsApp or phone 'customer' poses as a government office or event organiser. They place a large order, sometimes with a forged Local Order (LO). Then they ask for extra items the business does not make and refer the owner to a fake 'supplier', who demands upfront payment into personal or mule accounts. Then everyone disappears. Victims are bakeries, caterers, kuih makers, flower and gift shops, and a printing shop. Losses run from several thousand ringgit up to a business's whole savings. Food prepared for fake orders is also wasted.
pains.who: Micro and small F&B (bakeries, caterers), gift and flower shops, printing and stationery shops, and small trading firms that sell to government agencies and take orders on WhatsApp.

evidence.what_it_says: Perak police received "seven reports of fraud" from bakeries and caterers, with "losses of over RM300,000". Scammers place a sizeable order, then ask for extra items "usually ones not produced by the business operator" and refer victims to a supplier that demands upfront payment. Police: "after the payment was made, the individuals could no longer be contacted."

A 52-year-old Raub photocopy/printer business owner lost RM315,963 of "the victim's business savings". The scammer claimed to be from PPD Kuala Kangsar, sent a 'local order (LO)' and pointed her to a fake supplier. She paid RM18,498, then RM254,970, then RM42,495. Her request for the supplier's registration and TIN got no response.

Five Kuantan traders lost RM89,300 combined. Suspects posed as government representatives on phone and WhatsApp and ordered curtains, food, souvenirs and catering. They supplied a forged Local Order (LO) and vendor appointment letters, and directed payment to private bank accounts. Police: "a consistent modus operandi across the cases".

"FIVE small-scale traders specialising in flowers and gift items" in Miri lost more than RM28,000. Fake agency staff ordered 'door gifts', asked for items outside the victims' usual business and referred them to a 'supplier'. Payments went to mule accounts. Police advise confirming by phone or in person and say letterheads can be forged.

Headline: Johor police warn of a scam using the state police HQ's name after two caterers lost RM8,800 to fake orders. Per the search summary, the victims prepared meals and paid for 'souvenirs'. Details not verified by fetch.
Per the search summary, a trader lost over RM175,000 on a fictitious order linked to the Youth and Sports Ministry. Not fetched.

pains.frequency: New cases reported every few months across Pahang, Perak, Johor, Sarawak, Terengganu and KL (2025-2026). Each business screens incoming bulk orders weekly or more, but any one business is hit rarely.
pains.money_impact: RM8,800 (two Johor caterers) to RM315,963 (one Raub printing shop). Seven Perak cases exceeded RM300,000. Five Kuantan traders lost RM89,300.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Transfers to mule accounts are effectively irreversible. Perishable food prepared for fake orders is wasted. Event dates create urgency to pay the fake supplier fast.
pains.already_spending: unknown. Victims lodge police reports. Police advise manual verification by phone or visit, but no source shows owners paying for a verification tool.

pains.title: Fake transfer receipts and swapped QR codes at the counter: goods leave, money never arrives
pains.description: Customers show a screenshot of a 'successful' bank transfer, or a 'request for money' notification, and leave with goods before the trader checks the account. A variant: a fake customer pastes their own QR sticker over the shop's DuitNow QR, so later customers' payments go to the scammer. Each loss is small, but it happens at the point of sale in cash-light micro shops where the owner or a single cashier cannot check the bank app on every sale.
pains.who: Micro retailers, mini-markets, hawkers, restaurants and stalls that accept DuitNow QR or bank transfer at the counter. Also small landlords.

evidence.what_it_says: A Port Dickson supermarket trader lost RM780 of Nescafe and Milo. The pair switched from QR to bank transfer, "showed a receipt that looked successful" and left. When the trader checked later, "there was no credit transaction", only a "request for money" notification.

In Shah Alam, suspects showed a woman trader a screenshot of a digital receipt for RM304.50, but "no such payment had been transacted into her business account". Losses across two cases totalled RM348.10. Both suspects had prior records.

At a KL restaurant owned by Presma's deputy president, a fake customer stuck his own QR code over the counter's payment code while staff prepared his order. It was caught when a customer's payment did not arrive. A similar incident hit a Rawang outlet the day before. The owner said that if it had not been caught early, "the losses could have been significant".

evidence.source: The Star, citing Bukit Aman CCID
evidence.what_it_says: QR-code fraud: 223 cases / RM4.59mil in 2023, 655 / RM6.76mil in 2024, 5,907 / RM40.85mil in 2025, and 5,134 / RM28.67mil in Jan-Jun 2026. CAVEAT: the article describes 'quishing' to fake sites and payment gateways and does NOT say whether victims are merchants or consumers. Do not cite it as merchant losses.

evidence.source: MustShareNews, citing Sin Chew Daily (search result only)
evidence.what_it_says: Per the search summary, a Melaka landlord received a fake RM1,000 rent/deposit transfer screenshot. The couple allegedly used the same tactic on businesses in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka. Not fetched.

pains.frequency: The exposure happens on every transfer or QR sale, daily for micro retailers. Each reported loss is a single incident, and no merchant-specific frequency data exists.
pains.money_impact: RM300 to RM1,000 per reported incident. No aggregate figure for merchants. The national QR-fraud total (RM40.85mil in 2025) is not split by victim type.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Goods leave immediately, and the loss is discovered only when the account is checked later.
pains.already_spending: unknown. The implied cost is staff time to open the bank app and confirm each credit, but no source quantifies it.

pains.title: Supplier impersonation (business email compromise) redirects supplier payments to mule accounts
pains.description: Fraudsters pose as a known supplier by email and get the accounts staff to pay into mule accounts. Losses are large per incident. The firm usually discovers the fraud only when the real supplier asks to be paid. Messages often carry no malicious links, only plausible payment instructions.
pains.who: Small and medium manufacturers, distributors and logistics firms that pay suppliers by bank transfer, often run by one accounts clerk. Sources do not state company size, so micro relevance is unproven.

evidence.what_it_says: A Tangkak company "suffered losses exceeding RM700,000". A 60-year-old accounts officer corresponded with a fake steel supplier by email and made two payments "into accounts believed to be mule accounts". She found the forgery only when she checked the supplier's real email. Company size is not stated.

evidence.source: The Vibes, citing Kaspersky (private vendor data)
evidence.what_it_says: Malaysian firms lost "losses exceeding RM7.5 million to business email compromise (BEC) scams" between 2023 and 1H 2025. They faced "64,778 phishing attempts", "averaging over 5,300 incidents a month in 2024". Affected sectors: logistics, manufacturing and home appliance production. SMEs are not mentioned specifically.

pains.frequency: Over 5,300 phishing attempts a month against Malaysian companies (2024, Kaspersky). Successful frauds per firm are rare.
pains.money_impact: Over RM700,000 in a single 2026 case. Over RM7.5mil nationally from 2023 to 1H 2025 (Kaspersky).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: The real supplier is still owed, so the firm pays twice or risks stock-out. Funds are lost once moved through mule accounts.
pains.already_spending: unknown

pains.title: Cost squeeze after SST expansion, wage rises and new statutory contributions, with extra admin
pains.description: From 2025 onward, the July 2025 SST expansion (including 8% on commercial rent above landlord thresholds), the RM1,700 minimum wage and 2% EPF for foreign workers stacked onto F&B and services margins. Most businesses report higher costs and thinner margins, and about half report heavier administrative work from the tax changes. F&B operators report 10-30% input cost rises in 2026. Budget 2027 exempts MSMEs under RM50m sales from the next wage hike, which removes one future cost.
pains.who: F&B outlets, labour-heavy services and retail. The ACCCIM survey covers businesses broadly, with no micro-only split.

evidence.what_it_says: After the SST expansion: higher costs for 79.5% of businesses, reduced profit margins for 67.8%, and a heavier administrative burden for "nearly 50%" (49.1% per the search snippet). Sample size not stated.

evidence.source: ACCCIM M-BECS full report PDF (search result, not fetched)
evidence.what_it_says: Primary report behind the figures above. Per the search summary, 54.6% plan to pass costs to consumers and 44.6% plan to absorb them.

Per the search summary, Presma said operators face cost increases of 10 to 30 percent from supply-chain disruption, logistics, packaging, cooking gas and utilities. KPDN warned against unjustified price rises under the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering Act 2011. Not fetched.
Minimum wage set at RM1,700 from Feb 2025, with employers of fewer than five workers given until Aug 2025, per search summary. SME groups asked for a delay.

Per the search summary, mandatory EPF contributions for foreign workers start with October 2025 wages, at 2% employer and 2% employee, due by the 15th of the following month. No SME-burden figures were found.

pains.frequency: Monthly (payroll, EPF due on the 15th, SST filing, rent, utilities). Input prices change weekly in F&B.
pains.money_impact: 79.5% report higher costs and 67.8% thinner margins (ACCCIM 2025). F&B input costs are up 10-30% (Presma, 2026; snippet only).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Monthly statutory contribution and tax due dates. Price-increase enforcement risk under the Anti-Profiteering Act if menu prices rise without justification.
pains.already_spending: About half report a heavier admin burden (ACCCIM). Firms pass costs on through price increases (54.6%) or absorb them (44.6%, snippet). No accountant-fee figures were found.

pains.title: Delivery and marketplace fees take a large, rising cut of every order
pains.description: Food-delivery platforms take about 25-32% commission per order in Malaysia, and up to 60% with promotions and marketing fees (Samenta, 2024). Merchants mark menu prices up 30-100% on apps. Marketplaces keep adding fees. Shopee added a 2-3% commission rise plus RM0.50 per order in July 2025, which small sellers say exceeds their profit on low-value items. TikTok Shop raises most category commissions from 31 Oct 2026. This pushes micro sellers toward direct WhatsApp ordering, which is manual and error-prone.
pains.who: Micro F&B outlets and hawkers on GrabFood, foodpanda and ShopeeFood. Micro online sellers on Shopee and TikTok Shop selling low-value goods.

evidence.source: Malay Mail, quoting Samenta (search summary; malaymail pages blocked fetch)
evidence.what_it_says: Samenta said merchants are charged "up to 32 per cent commission on every delivery", and up to 60 per cent with 'promotions' and 'marketing fees'. It urged consumers to buy direct.
Per the search summary, merchants "have no choice but to mark up the selling price on delivery apps by 30 to 100 per cent to stay marginally profitable".

Opposes a "2% to 3% increase in commission rates" and "a RM0.50 platform support fee per order (plus SST)" from 16 July 2025. "For these low-value orders, the RM0.50 fee alone is more than our profit." 844 signatures.

TikTok Shop Malaysia raises most category commissions from 31 Oct 2026. Examples: non-BXP Mall beauty from 18.90% to 20.52%, and BXP women's tops from 10.26% to 12.74%. A few essentials categories get cheaper.
Per the search summary, no platform publishes a rate card, and independent estimates cluster at 25-30% in Malaysia. Not fetched.

pains.frequency: Every order, daily.
pains.money_impact: 25-32% of order value per delivery, and up to 60% with promotions (Samenta 2024). RM0.50 per Shopee order plus 2-3 points of commission (2025).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: No fine. Being delisted or losing platform visibility means lost sales, so owners feel forced to stay on the platforms.
pains.already_spending: Yes, the commissions and fees themselves. Some merchants move to direct WhatsApp ordering and self-delivery.

pains.title: Labour shortage threatening F&B closures
pains.description: Industry groups say more than 600 Indian and Indian Muslim restaurants are near permanent closure because they cannot get workers. This is a business-survival pain. Software cannot supply workers, but it is evidence that owners need to run with fewer hands.
pains.who: Labour-intensive micro and small F&B, especially mamak and Indian restaurants.

evidence.source: The Vibes, citing Primas and Presma
evidence.what_it_says: "More than 600 Indian and Indian Muslim restaurants across Malaysia are reportedly on the brink of permanent closure". "An estimated 5,000 Malaysians who depend indirectly on the industry could lose their livelihoods." The cause given is lack of workers. These are industry-group claims.

pains.frequency: Daily (staffing every shift).
pains.money_impact: Risk of permanent closure for 600+ restaurants (industry claim). No RM figure.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Closure, or reduced operating hours.
pains.already_spending: unknown (foreign-worker levies and recruitment are not quantified in the sources found).

news.context_notes:
MOST IMPORTANT, E-INVOICING IS LARGELY NO LONGER A SUPER PAIN FOR MICRO/SMALL FIRMS. LHDN raised the mandatory e-invoice threshold from RM1mil to RM3mil, effective 1 Sept 2026. "More than 1.1 million businesses" now qualify for the exemption (The Star, 30 Aug 2026: https://thestar.com.my/news/nation/2026/08/30/over-11-million-businesses-to-benefit-from-higher-e-invoicing-threshold-says-lhdn). Earlier, in Jan 2026, the RM1m-RM5m group was deferred a year with no penalty, and FMM said SMEs were not ready for a costly rollout (Malay Mail 5 Jan 2026, fetch blocked; NST https://www.nst.com.my/amp/business/corporate/2026/01/1351058/e-invoicing-deferment-provides-much-needed-headroom-smes-%E2%80%93-fmm). In July 2026 the PM said voluntary e-invoice corrections carry no penalty until 31 Dec 2027 (https://www.nst.com.my/amp/news/nation/2026/07/1482501/updated-anwar-no-e-invoicing-penalties-voluntary-corrections-until-dec). Penalties of RM200 to RM20,000 per offence appear only in a CFOtech article, not verified. The current deadline for firms between RM3m and RM5m is unclear, so check hasil.gov.my. Do not build the idea around mandatory e-invoicing for micro firms.

BUDGET 2027 (tabled 9 Oct 2026): RM57bil in MSME financing and guarantees, a 1-point corporate tax cut, and the minimum wage rising to RM2,000 from June 2027, but MSMEs with sales under RM50mil are exempt. A search snippet also reports the SST exemption threshold raised to RM1.5mil (Jan 2026), not verified. The think tank Insap says the budget does not fix cash flow.

DIGITAL ADOPTION CONTEXT (supports a 'shared hub' angle): KRI discussion paper, 24 May 2026 (https://www.krinstitute.org/publications/from-survival-to-scale-digital-empowerment-for-malaysias-micro-and-small-enterprises). Adoption among micro and small firms is "broad but shallow". Tools are concentrated "in sales, marketing, and payments". "Back-end processes remain less digitalised". "Digital tools are often implemented in isolation, with limited integration across business functions." Two more figures are search snippets only, not fetched. First, the Samenta/Ipsos SME Outlook Survey (Oct 2025): nearly 30% of SMEs still operate manually. Second, UOB Business Outlook Study 2026 (268 Malaysian SMEs): digital adoption slowed, and success rates have not changed since 2023.

CROSS-CUTTING PATTERN: pains 2, 3 and 4 (fake receipts or QR swaps, fake government or bulk orders, supplier impersonation) share one root failure. Money or goods move on unverified chat or email messages and screenshots, before anyone confirms against the bank account or the real counterparty. Police advice in every case is manual verification (call the agency, check the account credit, check supplier details and TIN). That points to a 'verify before money or goods move' workflow, which a shared business hub could own. Victims in the fake-order cases are clearly micro firms (bakeries, caterers, flower and gift shops, a printing shop). Size is unknown in the email-compromise (BEC) case.

FOOD WASTE / INVENTORY: no Malaysian news money figure was found for micro F&B. Only academic and vendor material appeared: an IRMA 2025 book chapter puts food waste at 23,000 tonnes per day, and a hospitality case study puts the loss at 23% of food purchase value. These are search snippets, not verified, so food waste is not included as a pain. Fake catering orders do cause prepared-food waste (Perak, Johor and PichaEats cases).

SIZE CAVEAT: Experian, Samenta and ACCCIM report SMEs as an aggregate, with no micro-only split. MAMBA's 60-120 day figure is the FocusM article's framing, not a measured statistic.

pains.title: Fake bulk orders and 'deposit-and-ditch' customers hit caterers, bakers and home food sellers
pains.description: Caterers, bakeries, kuih sellers and home food businesses take large orders by phone, WhatsApp or social media with no structured check on the buyer and often no deposit. Two loss patterns repeat. (a) Scam syndicates pose as a government agency, police HQ or university and place a big order. They then ask the business to prepay a fake 'second supplier' for items it does not make. (b) Real or fake buyers vanish or cancel after the food is cooked. Police advice is the same manual checklist each time: verify the buyer, meet in person, take a deposit. This is a money-losing pain tied to the busywork of taking orders by chat.
pains.who: Micro and small caterers, bakeries, kuih and home-based food sellers. Peaks at Ramadan/Raya and before events. Evidence is Malaysia-specific.

evidence.what_it_says: Bukit Aman CCID: 241 cases in 2025 with losses of over RM8 million, and 80 cases nationwide so far in 2026 with losses of RM1.9 million. Suspects pose as government agencies or companies and place bulk orders for souvenirs or food supplies. Quote: 'They call to order souvenirs or food, claim to be from enforcement agencies or organisations'. The category is souvenir plus food-supply scams, not only F&B.

Seven reports to Perak police, losses over RM300,000, victims were bakeries and catering businesses. The suspect orders set quantities, then asks for extra items the business does not make, then gives a 'supplier' number that demands upfront payment.

evidence.source: RTM, Malay (search-result summary only, not fetched)
evidence.what_it_says: Per the search summary, the method has been tracked since last year, with 66 cases recorded in Perak. Police advise wariness about unusual orders, meeting customers in person and taking deposits. Unverified: page not opened.
A food supply company and a catering company lost a total of RM8,800 to a syndicate impersonating the Johor police HQ (IPK). Police said they issued no such orders.

A Penampang caterer prepared 150 lunch sets for a buyer claiming to be an army officer. The buyer refused a deposit and offered cash on delivery, then deleted the WhatsApp messages and blocked her. The district CCID had received several reports of similar scams. Dated 2023.

A Shah Alam home seller made 30 packs of doughnuts (RM300). The customer refused a deposit and cancelled at delivery with 'I would like to cancel la, dik. Bye'. The order came via Facebook Messenger. Anecdotal and dated.

pains.frequency: Per business: occasional, with seasonal peaks (Ramadan/Raya, event season). Nationally: 241 reported cases in 2025 (about 4-5 per week, reported cases only). The underlying order-taking and deposit-chasing over chat is daily.
pains.money_impact: Per case from RM300 (one cancelled home order) to tens of thousands. One Perak cluster lost over RM300,000 across 7 reports (2026). Nationally over RM8 million in 2025 (souvenir plus food-supply scams combined).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Forced consequence: food is cooked for a fixed event date and spoils or is dumped if the buyer vanishes. Prepayments to the fake supplier are unrecoverable.
pains.already_spending: Owners absorb the losses and file police reports. No evidence found of paid tools for this. Police advice (deposits, in-person verification) is manual effort.

pains.title: Confirming payment by hand: fake transfer receipts and QR-code swaps at the counter and on WhatsApp
pains.description: Small shops, stalls and chat-based sellers accept DuitNow QR and bank transfers. Most confirm payment by eye: a screenshot or a 'successful' screen on the customer's phone. Checking the bank app for every transaction is manual and gets skipped when the shop is busy. Fraudsters use this gap with edited transfer receipts and by pasting their own QR code over the merchant's. The merchant often finds out only when reconciling later.
pains.who: Micro retailers (sundry shops, mini markets), restaurants and stalls, and WhatsApp/Instagram/Facebook sellers who take payment off-platform. Evidence is Malaysia-specific.

evidence.what_it_says: A Port Dickson trader lost RM780 of Nescafé and Milo after a couple showed a fake 'successful' transfer receipt. 'When we checked the account, there was no credit transaction — just a request for money notification.' The trader admitted the payment was not verified immediately.

At a KL restaurant owned by Presma's deputy president, a man covered the counter QR code with his own. It was discovered when a customer's payment did not show in the restaurant's account. A similar incident was reported in Rawang the day before. The owner said 'Imagine if he managed to do this at dozens of restaurants — it could add up'.
Lists 'Fake Payment Proof' on Facebook Marketplace and WhatsApp (edited transfer screenshots) as a common scam for Malaysian sellers: 'Never rely on screenshots alone.' No statistics cited.
Says many small sellers confirm payment via WhatsApp bank details and screenshots, which are easy to fake. Its RM8,500 Maybank2u screenshot example is illustrative, not a reported case.

evidence.source: The Sun (search-result summary only, not fetched)
evidence.what_it_says: Per the search summary, a police-linked advisory calls fake payment receipts a common tactic against traders and suggests DuitNow QR Soundbox devices to confirm payments. Unverified wording.

pains.frequency: Every transfer or QR payment, daily. Fraud incidents per shop are occasional.
pains.money_impact: Reported single incidents range from RM6.60 (QR swap) to RM780 (fake receipt). No national figure found specific to merchant receipt fraud.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Goods are handed over or shipped immediately, so a missed check is an instant, unrecoverable loss.
pains.already_spending: Some merchants buy soundbox devices (suggested by the police-linked advisory, unverified). Otherwise staff time is spent checking bank apps and reconciling at day end.

pains.title: Volatile supplier and ingredient prices squeeze F&B margins; owners re-price and re-order by gut
pains.description: Vegetable, egg, flour and other input prices move sharply, sometimes doubling or tripling within weeks. Small operators mostly absorb the rise because they cannot see cost per dish or reprice quickly. They react by buying only 1-2 days of stock, swapping ingredients or shrinking portions. Any price change also has to appear on price tags and menus: KPDN compounds traders for missing or incomplete price displays.
pains.who: Kopitiam, mamak, tomyam, stalls, caterers, cafes and home bakers, mainly micro and small. Malaysia-specific.

evidence.what_it_says: Presma VP: 'Two months ago, 1kg of mustard greens cost RM2.50 to RM3; now it is RM6 to RM7.' A Kota Baru owner reports red chillies at RM12-RM14 rising to up to RM25-RM30/kg and water spinach at about RM3-RM3.50 rising to about RM18/kg. Presma members buy only one or two days' worth of stock to limit waste. 'Customers rarely feel the impact because we cushion it.'

Tomyam operators' adviser: 'Prices of raw ingredients have already gone up by 10% to 20% since the start of the year.' Kangkung/kailan at RM7-RM9/kg versus RM2.50 and RM4.60 previously. Primas: supplies now carry SST of 6% or 8%, and 'many members have tried to maintain their prices in spite of escalating costs, but this is no longer possible.'

evidence.source: Asia News Network / The Star (search-result summary only, not fetched)
evidence.what_it_says: After the egg subsidy ended on 1 Aug 2025, a JB takoyaki seller reports egg trays rising from around RM9 to RM12.99. A caterer uses fewer eggs in bulk bee hoon to match customer budgets.

evidence.source: The Sun via Newswav (search-result summary only, not fetched)
evidence.what_it_says: Per the search summary, the Malaysian Food and Beverage Executives Association said 30% to 35% of new F&B ventures shut within 12 to 18 months, citing limited pricing power and poor capital planning. Association observation, not a formal survey.
Per the search summary, Retail Group Malaysia reported cafe and restaurant sales fell 4.6% in Q1 2026 year on year. Restaurants are shrinking portions.

Per the search summary, KPDN Johor recorded 123 cases with compounds of RM13,300 under the Price Control and Anti-Profiteering Act during the Raya 2025 scheme. The most frequent offence was a missing price tag. Not eatery-specific.
A Sarawak eatery was fined RM300 under the 2020 Price Marking Order for not displaying menu prices. Dated precedent.

pains.frequency: Purchasing is daily or every 1-2 days. Price swings arrive in waves of weeks (monsoon Nov-Dec, subsidy changes, fuel).
pains.money_impact: Input costs up 10-20% in H1 2025 (tomyam operators). Single vegetables up 2-6x in the late-2025 monsoon. Margins are absorbed by owners. 30-35% of new F&B ventures close within 12-18 months (association claim).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: KPDN compounds for missing or incomplete price displays (examples RM200-RM300 per eatery; the Act allows much higher). Over-buying perishables means spoilage.
pains.already_spending: Owners absorb the costs and spend time sourcing alternatives and repricing. No evidence found of paid costing tools among micro operators.

pains.title: Marketplace fee creep (Shopee, TikTok Shop) eats online sellers' margins, and sellers can't see true profit per order
pains.description: Shopee and TikTok Shop have added or raised several fees in 2024-2026: transaction fee, SPayLater fee, commission revisions, a per-order platform support fee and possibly a 5% technical support fee. Each deduction is small and changes on a different date, so small sellers struggle to know their real margin per SKU and when to reprice. Sellers say they will raise prices or move away from the platform.
pains.who: Micro and small online sellers on Shopee and TikTok Shop in Malaysia.

evidence.what_it_says: Shopee's SPayLater seller fee rose from 3.5% to 4.5% from 8 May 2025, and sellers cannot opt out. The transaction fee had already risen from 2% to 3.5% in August 2024. Sellers suggested raising prices. One said rising costs push him 'away from focusing too much effort towards selling in Shopee.'
New Platform Support Fee of RM0.50 excluding SST (RM0.54 including) per successfully delivered order. Delivered orders that are later returned or refunded are still charged.

A TikTok Shop Malaysia programme seller pays about 18.9% of order value (commission about 10.26%, Bonus Cashback about 4.86%, transaction about 3.78%, SST-inclusive) plus RM0.54 per order. Outside the programme, about 14% plus RM0.54.

Example for a RM100 electronics order: commission 6% + SST on commission RM0.48 + transaction 2.16% + 5% technical support fee = RM13.64 deducted. Commission rose on 1 Feb and again on 21 May 2026. Claims the 5% fee applies to local sellers with 'No exceptions.'
This contradicts Jumix: 'the 5% technical support fee are applicable to CB sellers only (Not local sellers in the respective markets)'. Whether local Malaysian sellers pay the 5% fee is unverified.

pains.frequency: Every order. Fee rules changed several times a year (Aug 2024, May 2025, Feb 2026, May 2026).
pains.money_impact: Roughly 12-19% of order value on TikTok Shop plus RM0.54 per order (vendor estimates). Shopee example: RM13.64 per RM100 electronics order if the 5% fee applies. Affiliate commissions and ads come on top.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: No penalty. Fee changes take effect on fixed dates, and sellers who do not reprice lose margin on every order from that date.
pains.already_spending: Yes: fees are deducted automatically. Sellers also pay for ERP and fee-calculator tools (BigSeller, Inseller), which shows existing spend.

pains.title: Marketplace shipping deadlines and penalty points: late shipment, overselling cancellations and return windows
pains.description: Shopee scores sellers on rolling 7-day metrics: Late Shipment Rate, Non-Fulfilment Rate and, from May 2026, Fast Handover Rate. Breaches add penalty points that can suspend seller privileges for up to 28 days. Sellers who list the same stock on several platforms have no native stock sync, so overselling causes cancellations that count against them. TikTok Shop reportedly auto-approves refunds if the seller does not respond within 48 hours. Tracking this across platforms from a phone is constant busywork with a hard penalty.
pains.who: Micro and small multi-channel online sellers (Shopee, TikTok Shop, Lazada) in Malaysia.

evidence.what_it_says: LSR is the share of orders shipped after the deadline over the past 7 days. Thresholds were loosened to 15%/10% from 11 Feb 2026, then returned to 10% (regular) and 5% (Mall/Preferred) from 8 Apr 2026. LSR of 10% or more gives 1 point (2 points with 50 or more late orders). Points can lead to suspension of seller privileges for up to 28 days.
Per the search summary, Fast Handover Rate joins the Seller Penalty Points system from 11 May 2026. NFR (seller-fault cancellations and returns) should stay below 10%.

Shopee, Lazada and TikTok Shop have no native cross-platform stock sync, so a unit sold on one platform can still show as available on another. Cancellations from overselling count toward cancellation-rate thresholds.
TikTok Shop sellers must handle return/refund requests within 48 hours, otherwise the refund is auto-approved. Not verified against TikTok's own policy.

pains.frequency: Daily shipping cut-offs. Metrics are recalculated on a rolling 7 days.
pains.money_impact: Not quantified. Suspension for up to 28 days or removal from Mall/Preferred programmes cuts sales. Auto-approved refunds lose both goods and payment.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Hard ship-by deadlines, penalty points, privilege suspension for up to 28 days, programme offboarding, and a 48-hour refund response window (TikTok, unverified).
pains.already_spending: Sellers buy ERP/OMS tools (BigSeller and others) mainly for stock sync and order handling. Exact spend unknown.

pains.title: Food-delivery commissions take 15-30% of every order; restaurants push customers to WhatsApp ordering, which brings back manual order-taking
pains.description: GrabFood, foodpanda and ShopeeFood commissions take a large share of each delivery order. Small F&B owners often move regulars to direct WhatsApp or website ordering to avoid the fees. That brings back manual work: taking orders, confirming payment and dispatching. Note: most current commission figures come from vendors that sell alternatives.
pains.who: Small restaurants, cafes, cloud kitchens and home food sellers in Malaysia.

evidence.what_it_says: GrabFood 15-22% depending on tier, foodpanda 12-20%, ShopeeFood 10-18%. Worked example: at RM60,000 monthly delivery GMV, fees are RM10,800 at 18%.
foodpanda and GrabFood charged 25-35% per order, smaller local platforms 10-20%. A 30% commission is now 'about one-third revenue for many restaurants.' Dated.
Per the search summary, KPDNHEP logged 1,903 complaints about foodpanda in 2020 and 946 in Jan-Aug 2021. The ministry raised delays in paying traders and high commissions with the platforms. Dated.

evidence.source: Jumix Design blog (vendor, search-result summary only)
evidence.what_it_says: GrabFood/foodpanda commissions commonly 15%-30% per order. F&B brands cut cost by taking orders through their own website or WhatsApp and using delivery apps only for delivery.

pains.frequency: Every delivery order, daily.
pains.money_impact: 15-30% of delivery revenue. Example: RM10,800 per month on RM60,000 GMV at 18% (vendor example).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: None direct. Orders and payments not confirmed in time on WhatsApp mean lost or late orders (no data found).
pains.already_spending: Yes: commissions plus optional monthly subscription tiers (GrabFood Plus, foodpanda Premium; amounts not stated).

pains.title: Supplier ordering over WhatsApp plus manual stock-taking leads to over-ordering, spoilage and paper-invoice backlogs
pains.description: Small F&B outlets order from many suppliers by WhatsApp or phone, often daily. They track stock by eye or paper, and supplier invoices arrive as photos or handwritten delivery notes. The result is over-ordering and spoilage, or stock-outs, plus hours of re-keying for whoever does the books. Evidence on the money size of this pain is weak and mostly dated or from vendors.
pains.who: Restaurants, cafes, kopitiam, caterers and central-kitchen franchises, from micro to small. Malaysia plus regional vendor commentary.

evidence.what_it_says: Food Market Hub founders (Malaysia): one restaurant can need roughly 200 purchase orders a month, and complexity rises sharply with a central kitchen. The platform served about 2,000 outlets in MY/SG/HK/TW. Dated.
Presma members tightened stock management and buy only one or two days' worth of stock to limit waste. This implies frequent, small re-orders.

evidence.source: Ajinomoto Food Biz Partner (industry content, fetched)
evidence.what_it_says: Calls poor inventory tracking a hidden cost for Malaysian cafes and restaurants, causing waste, spoilage and over-ordering: 'Without accurate records, purchasing decisions become less reliable.' No figures.

evidence.source: Peakflo blog (vendor, REGIONAL SEA, search-result summary only)
evidence.what_it_says: WhatsApp works as the procurement workflow in SEA F&B. Supplier documents arrive as WhatsApp photos, PDFs and handwritten notes keyed in by hand. Claims 100+ finance hours a month on invoice entry (unverified vendor figure, likely for larger groups).
SWCorp: edible food wastage about 5,000 tonnes/day in 2024, rising to about 6,000 tonnes/day in 2025. Restaurants and canteens are named among sources, with no restaurant-specific figure.
Malaysian restaurant owners estimated 10% to 30% of cooked food is thrown away daily. Very dated, anecdotal.

pains.frequency: Supplier orders daily or every 1-2 days. About 200 POs a month per restaurant (2020 founder claim).
pains.money_impact: Unknown for micro/small firms in 2024-2026. Only dated anecdotal estimates of 10-30% cooked-food waste (2011).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Perishables spoil within days. A stock-out means dishes cannot be sold that day.
pains.already_spending: Some outlets pay for procurement/inventory SaaS (Food Market Hub). Others spend staff and owner hours. Spend among micro firms unknown.

pains.title: Cash stuck in receivables: caterers and suppliers to corporate or government clients wait 60-120 days
pains.description: Small firms that sell B2B, such as caterers for corporate or government events and food suppliers to restaurants, deliver first and get paid much later. They chase payment by hand over WhatsApp and phone. This is less relevant to marketplace sellers, whose Shopee escrow reportedly releases within about 3 days.
pains.who: Micro and small caterers and food or packaging suppliers with B2B or government customers. Malaysia-specific.

evidence.what_it_says: SME payment delays fell from 69 days (2022) to 64 days (early 2025), against 58 days for large corporations. The corporate-SME gap in hospitality is 13 days and in wholesale 10 days (1Q 2025). CEO: 'many SMEs remain highly exposed to cash flow gaps.'

evidence.source: The Sun (search-result summary only, not fetched)
evidence.what_it_says: The Malaysian Micro Business Association (Mamba) says micro and small enterprises often deliver upfront but are paid 60 to 120 days later. Only an estimated 3% of receivables are captured by factoring (citing AFS Alliance).
The caterer accepted no deposit because 'government orders are typically paid only after fulfilment'. Shows payment-after-delivery is the norm for this segment.
Counterpoint for online sellers: Shopee escrow is released within 3 days of delivery, or within 24 hours if the buyer confirms receipt.

pains.frequency: Monthly billing and chasing cycles. Every B2B job.
pains.money_impact: Working capital tied up for about 64 days on average (SMEs, Experian), and 60-120 days per Mamba. No ringgit totals for micro firms found.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Suppliers and wages must still be paid on time while receivables are outstanding. Consequence is a cash crunch (not quantified).
pains.already_spending: Some use factoring (only about 3% of receivables per Mamba claim). Otherwise owner time spent chasing.

pains.title: Recurring compliance deadlines for small F&B: food-handler typhoid jabs and training, and e-invoicing for RM1m-RM5m firms from 2027
pains.description: F&B owners must make sure every food handler has a typhoid vaccination and certified training. Health inspectors issue compounds and can order closures. Staff turnover makes this a tracking chore. Separately, firms with RM1m-RM5m in annual sales face mandatory e-invoicing after the 2026 penalty-free year, which runs to 2027 and is about two months away from today (2026-10-24). Retail is now allowed consolidated e-invoices. Firms under RM1m are exempt.
pains.who: All food premises including stalls and bazaar traders (health rules). Small F&B and retail firms with RM1m-RM5m in sales (e-invoicing). Malaysia-specific.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (search-result summary only; site blocks fetch)
evidence.what_it_says: Kedah Health Department issued 112 compounds worth RM14,000 after inspecting 80 Ramadan bazaar sites. 3% of food handlers lacked anti-typhoid vaccination and 10% had not attended mandatory food-handler training.

MOH: stall operators must ensure all handlers are vaccinated and trained at ministry-recognised schools. Penalties include closure orders of up to 14 days under Section 11 of the Food Act 1983 and fines under the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009.
MOH issued 1,639 notices at Ramadan bazaars, with compound values of RM163,900, covering failures such as no food-handler training or no typhoid vaccination.
The mandatory e-invoicing deadline for companies with RM1 million to RM5 million in annual sales is extended to 2027, giving time to comply without penalties.
Businesses below RM1 million in revenue are exempt (threshold raised from RM500,000 in Dec 2025). Consolidated e-invoicing is extended to the retail and building-materials sectors.

Firms using relaxation measures still submit consolidated e-invoices monthly. Interim relaxation ends 31 Dec 2027. A separate search summary cited fines of RM200-RM20,000 per non-compliance, but which source said this is unclear, so it is unverified.

pains.frequency: Health: continuous as staff join or leave; certificate renewals (typhoid every 3 years per a non-official site, unverified). E-invoicing: per sale or monthly consolidated.
pains.money_impact: Compounds of about RM100-RM125 each (Kedah 2026: RM14,000 over 112 compounds; MOH 2024: RM163,900 over 1,639 notices). Closure for up to 14 days means lost sales. E-invoice fines unverified.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Health compounds and closure orders of up to 14 days. E-invoicing becomes mandatory for RM1m-RM5m firms in 2027 after the penalty-free period.
pains.already_spending: Owners pay for staff jabs and training courses. Businesses buy e-invoice/POS software (capital allowance announced for e-invoice spend). Amounts not found.
