pains.title: Customers pay late, so cash sits unpaid for about 2 months and chasing it is manual
pains.description: Malaysian SMEs wait longer to be paid than large corporates do, and owners name cash flow as a top pressure. Experian reports SME payment delays averaged 64 days in early 2025. A 2023 regional survey found that following up on late payments was the most widespread receivables problem, with manual invoicing and manual reminders still common. Accounting tools (Bukku, SQL, AutoCount and others) record the invoice, but none of the sources show a tool that runs the follow-up for a micro firm. Orbyte's own platform page lists 'follow up unpaid invoices' only as a future AI example, not a shipped feature. Caveat: Experian's 'SME' figures include medium firms. No source splits out micro or small firms.
pains.who: Micro and small B2B suppliers selling on credit terms, mostly in transport/logistics, hospitality, wholesale and services. These owners chase payment themselves.

evidence.what_it_says: SME payment delays fell from 69 days in 2022 to 64 days in early 2025. Large corporations averaged 58 days. CEO Dawn Lai: 'many SMEs remain highly exposed to cash flow gaps.'

Q1 2025 SME-to-corporate payment gaps: transport/logistics 26 days (average delay 76 days), hospitality 13 days, wholesale 10 days. Lai warns of 'delayed expansion plans, tighter supplier terms, and even higher borrowing costs.'

evidence.source: New Straits Times (SME Association of Malaysia survey)
evidence.what_it_says: Only 9.8% of respondents called their cash flow healthy. 49% said they were under pressure and may need financing support.
April 2026 survey: 45% feared 'serious cash flow problems if current market conditions persist'. The association asked for 'faster payment mechanisms to improve liquidity' in procurement.

evidence.source: Funding Societies (REGIONAL: ~1,000 SMEs in ID, MY, SG, TH, VN)
evidence.what_it_says: Following up on late payments was the most widespread receivables issue in the region. Processing sales orders was the second-biggest concern in Malaysia. The post mentions manual invoicing and manual reminders. It gives no Malaysia percentages.
Lists 'follow up unpaid invoices' and a Business Graph that links invoices, payment terms and cash flow. Both are framed as future-state direction, not finished features.

pains.frequency: Continuous: it applies to every credit sale. Average SME delay is 64 days (Experian, early 2025). No source measures how often owners chase payment.
pains.money_impact: Cash is locked for about 64 days per invoice on average, and up to 26 days longer than corporates wait in logistics. No source gives a ringgit figure per firm.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Experian warns of tighter supplier terms, delayed expansion and higher borrowing costs. 49% of surveyed SMEs say they may need financing support (July 2026).
pains.already_spending: Unknown direct spend on collections. Indirect spend: financing costs, plus bookkeeping services quoted at RM500-RM2,000/month by an accounting vendor (see bookkeeping pain).

pains.title: Exempt micro and small suppliers face withheld payments when large buyers demand e-invoices
pains.description: LHDN raised the e-invoice exemption threshold to RM3 million turnover in General Guideline v4.8 (30 Aug 2026). Most micro and small firms are now exempt. SME associations report that larger, e-invoice-ready customers still ask exempt suppliers for TIN, SSM and SST details, and that some delay payment because no e-invoice is issued. LHDN says normal receipts remain valid proof of expense, so the pressure comes from buyer confusion, not from the law. Self-billed e-invoices are also widely misunderstood. Accounting and middleware vendors sell e-invoice modules, but the sources show nothing that helps an exempt seller prove exemption or answer buyer requests quickly. Firms at or above RM3M, and subsidiaries of RM3M+ groups, remain in scope.
pains.who: Micro and small suppliers under RM3M turnover selling B2B to larger companies. Also small firms at or above RM3M, or inside RM3M+ groups, that must comply.

evidence.date: 2026-09-04 (page date. Related headlines on the page are dated October 2026, so the date is unconfirmed)
evidence.what_it_says: Dr Chin Chee Seong (SME Association of Malaysia) warns of exempt SMEs 'payments being delayed simply because they are not issuing e-invoices'. William Ng (Samenta) says larger clients 'were actively asking some exempt suppliers for information' such as TIN, SSM number and sales tax details. Datin Christine Koh: the threshold went from RM150,000 to RM500,000 to RM1mil and now RM3mil. Some firms 'may now find themselves exempt after already incurring these costs.'

evidence.source: JomEInvoice (third-party summary of LHDN guideline v4.8)
evidence.what_it_says: Exemption covers 'annual turnover or revenue of less than RM3,000,000'. The carve-outs cover non-individual shareholders, holding companies and related companies at or above RM3M. Relaxation period runs to 31 Dec 2027, with penalty enforcement from 1 Jan 2028. 'Your normal receipts remain valid proof of expense for buyers.'
LHDN: 'taxpayers can continue to claim tax deductions or personal tax relief using existing documentation' such as a normal bill, receipt or invoice.
Datuk Koong Lin Loong (ACCCIM): 'Many of them are still struggling to understand self-billed invoices.' FMBA expects SMEs and micro-businesses to face greater difficulties.
Samenta's William Ng estimated e-invoicing could cost 'up to RM200,000 per SME in the first year' and up to RM50,000 a year after that. This is an association estimate for in-scope SMEs.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (headline and search snippet only; the page returned 403)
evidence.what_it_says: Headline: 'Higher threshold, same headache: SMEs push for simpler tax reporting'. The search snippet says larger e-invoicing companies may impose extra requirements on exempt micro-businesses that could delay payments to them. I could not read the full text.

evidence.source: CFOtech Asia (quotes a QuickBooks spokesperson, so vendor-sourced)
evidence.what_it_says: Non-compliance with e-invoicing: RM200 up to RM20,000 per offence.

pains.frequency: Unknown. The association statements imply it arises on each sale to an e-invoice-ready corporate buyer.
pains.money_impact: Payments delayed or withheld (no ringgit figure). In-scope compliance cost estimated at up to RM200,000 in year one (Samenta, 2024, association estimate).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: In-scope firms: RM200-RM20,000 per offence after the relaxation period (enforcement from 1 Jan 2028). Exempt firms: withheld payments from buyers (no legal penalty).
pains.already_spending: Some SMEs already paid for e-invoice preparation and are now exempt (Koh, The Star). Vendors sell MyInvois modules. One unverified guide estimates RM100-300/month plus RM500-2,000 setup.

pains.title: Back-office records stay manual, so owners pay accountants and lose access to financing
pains.description: Micro and small firms digitise the front office (payments, online presence) while bookkeeping and records stay manual. Khazanah Research Institute and MDEC (May 2026) cite 'limited documentation, weak record-keeping'. Owners then pay outside bookkeepers and tax agents to rebuild the books. Weak documentation has been cited as a top reason SME loan applications are rejected, but that evidence is older. Accounting software exists, including a free Bukku plan, but these sources show adoption stays shallow.
pains.who: Micro firms and sole proprietors, plus small Sdn Bhd owners who outsource bookkeeping, tax filing and company secretarial work.

evidence.source: Khazanah Research Institute and MDEC discussion paper
evidence.what_it_says: Adoption is 'concentrated in front-facing and transactional activities'. Back-end processes often 'remain manual'. Many MSMEs have 'limited documentation, weak record-keeping'. 'Fragmentation across programmes and agencies increases the cost of access for smaller firms.'

evidence.source: Visa whitepaper press release (search snippet. Date not confirmed)
evidence.what_it_says: Only 46% of MSMEs use online solutions for finance and accounting.
Accounting and bookkeeping services 'usually start from RM500 and may go up to RM1,500 or RM2,000 per month'. A startup company pays roughly RM1,000-RM1,500 for tax services.
Insufficient documentation is cited as the top reason SME loan applications are turned down.
Misclassifying business expenses: RM5,000 to RM100,000 in overpaid taxes per year (vendor claim). Inconsistent cash-flow tracking can stall 20-30% of potential revenue growth (vendor claim).

pains.frequency: Monthly for bookkeeping (vendors quote monthly fees) and annually for tax filing.
pains.money_impact: RM300-RM2,000/month on outsourced bookkeeping (vendor quotes), plus RM1,000-1,500/year on tax services. Financing denied for lack of documents (no current figure).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Annual tax filing deadline (exact rule not verified in these sources). Loan rejection for insufficient documentation (older evidence).
pains.already_spending: Yes. Owners pay external bookkeepers, tax agents and company secretaries (RM80-200/month quoted by one provider).

pains.title: Marketplace sellers get penalised for late shipment caused by messy order and stock tracking
pains.description: Micro sellers on Shopee are scored on a rolling 7-day Late Shipment Rate. Since 8 April 2026 the threshold is 10% for regular sellers and 5% for Mall/Preferred sellers. Breaches add penalty points that can suspend seller privileges for up to 28 days. Preferred and Mall sellers can be offboarded. A seller-tools vendor names root causes such as 'disorganised inventory, missed cut-off times, and no clear order-monitoring process'. Sellers who also take WhatsApp orders juggle stock across channels. I found no source on cross-platform overselling or TikTok Shop penalties.
pains.who: Micro and small online sellers on Shopee, Lazada or TikTok Shop, often also selling on WhatsApp.

evidence.what_it_says: LSR thresholds were loosened to 15%/10% from 11 Feb 2026, then tightened back to 10% (regular) and 5% (Mall/Preferred) from 8 Apr 2026. LSR at or above 10% with fewer than 50 late orders gives 1 point, and 50 or more gives 2 points. Points can lead to 'suspension of seller privileges for up to 28 days'. The article names 'disorganised inventory, missed cut-off times, and no clear order-monitoring process' as causes.
Penalties are tiered from a warning to reduced visibility, restricted features and loss of campaign eligibility, up to suspending or closing the store.

evidence.source: Product listing for a WhatsApp order tool (vendor claim; search snippet)
evidence.what_it_says: Micro-sellers who sell through WhatsApp and Instagram DMs often lose orders in chat history or copy them by hand into Excel.

pains.frequency: Weekly: Shopee measures LSR over a rolling 7 days.
pains.money_impact: Lost visibility and campaign eligibility, or up to 28 days of suspended privileges. No ringgit figure was found.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Each order has a shipping deadline. Penalty points escalate to suspension or offboarding.
pains.already_spending: Some sellers pay for multichannel ERP tools such as BigSeller (vendor). Spend level unknown.

pains.title: Fake payment screenshots and QR swaps on WhatsApp and social selling
pains.description: Sellers who take orders on WhatsApp, Facebook or Instagram often accept a transfer screenshot as proof of payment. Fake receipts are easy to produce, and a police-linked official says AI can generate them. Sellers ship and lose the goods. A related scam replaces a merchant's printed DuitNow QR code, and the merchant only finds out when reconciling. WhatsApp Business and most POS tools do not check that a payment actually landed for each order, so owners check bank apps by hand. Magnitude is unknown: I found no official loss statistics.
pains.who: Micro sellers and F&B/market stalls that take orders or payments off-platform (WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, DuitNow QR).

evidence.source: Bernama (search snippet only; fetch failed, date unconfirmed)
evidence.what_it_says: A police-linked official says fake payment receipts are a common tactic against traders, and they can be generated with AI or bought on the dark web. He advises DuitNow QR soundboxes and verifying each transaction.
The scam 'usually happens when you're selling outside of official e-commerce platforms'. The buyer sends a screenshot, but 'the screenshot is edited or fake, no real money was sent.'

evidence.source: Curlec (payment vendor; illustrative scenario, not a documented case)
evidence.what_it_says: Scenario: a seller ships RM8,500 of stock after a convincing Maybank2u transfer screenshot. No payment arrives and the buyer disappears.
Scammers swap merchants' DuitNow QR codes. Merchants notice only when reconciling payments. The page claims over 2 billion DuitNow QR transactions in 2025.
35% lost time or money to a cyber-attack in 2025. Only 39% reviewed their cybersecurity protections. The context implies Malaysia but does not state it explicitly.

pains.frequency: Unknown. Exposure exists on every off-platform order paid by transfer.
pains.money_impact: Full value of goods shipped per incident. The only figure is a vendor's RM8,500 illustration. No aggregate data.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Goods lost and unrecoverable once shipped.
pains.already_spending: Some merchants buy DuitNow QR soundboxes, as police advise. Spend amount unknown.

pains.title: Cost spikes squeeze margins faster than owners can see or reprice (sharpest in F&B)
pains.description: SME Association surveys in 2026 show broad, steep cost increases. Owners do not see the margin hit until it is too late to reprice. F&B adds delivery-app commissions and imported-ingredient inflation. The 'no visibility' angle is inferred: the cost pressure is well evidenced, but I found no survey that measures owners' lack of cost visibility. F&B commission and margin figures come from a vendor with no cited sources.
pains.who: Micro and small F&B outlets, cafes, stalls, and other SMEs with volatile input costs (fuel, energy, ingredients).

evidence.source: New Straits Times (SME Association of Malaysia survey)
evidence.what_it_says: 83.3% of SMEs reported operating cost increases above 10%. 63.7% reported increases above 30%.
76% said rising fuel prices 'had severely impacted their operations'. More than 80% saw double-digit increases in operating costs.

evidence.source: The Star (Airwallex-commissioned survey by Vase.ai, 415 SMEs)
evidence.what_it_says: 67% cite rising costs as the top pressure and 42% cite managing cash flow. Barriers to tech adoption: high implementation costs 44%, data privacy 34%, lack of internal expertise 33%.

evidence.source: Klikit (restaurant software vendor; no sources cited, and it misstates the minimum wage, so reliability is low)
evidence.what_it_says: Net margins 5-15%. Commissions: GrabFood 12-18%, Foodpanda 10-15%, ShopeeFood 10-14%. 'Ingredient costs have risen 8-12% year-over-year.'
Foodpanda and GrabFood commissions put at 25-35% at the time, which triggered operator backlash.

evidence.source: Malay Mail citing RGM data (search snippet only)
evidence.what_it_says: Cafe and restaurant operators expect a further 2.3% decline in Q2 2026. 'Food away from home' prices rose 2.6% in April alone.

pains.frequency: Unknown for cost reviews. The cost increases themselves are ongoing (2026 surveys).
pains.money_impact: 63.7% of surveyed SMEs report cost increases above 30%. F&B net margins of 5-15% (vendor) leave little room.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: No hard deadline. Consequences are margin loss and possible cash-flow failure (45% anticipate difficulties within 3-6 months).
pains.already_spending: Delivery commissions, per the vendor figures above. No evidence of spend on cost-tracking tools.

pains.title: Available tools are costly, fragmented and shallowly adopted, and grants are slow to pay out
pains.description: Micro and small firms already use or can access accounting (Bukku free tier, SQL RM79/month, AutoCount RM2,800 one-off, Financio RM50/month), POS (Qashier about RM79/month, StoreHub and Eats365 about RM99/month per competitor comparisons) and grants. But their tech spend goes into hardware and customer-facing apps, not process automation or systems integration. Implementation cost and lack of expertise are the top barriers. The Geran Digital PMKS MADANI grant matches 50% up to RM5,000 and needs the owner to co-fund. A RM19 million payout backlog to digital partners was only cleared in May 2026. Note: Orbyte's own pitch (one hub for disconnected tools) targets this pain, so a 'connect everything' idea would overlap Orbyte Connect.
pains.who: Micro and small owners without IT staff, plus the digital-partner vendors who serve them.

evidence.source: CPA Australia Small Business Survey (Nov-Dec 2025 fieldwork; 4,166 firms in 11 markets)
evidence.what_it_says: Initiatives 'have yet to drive significant uptake of deeper productivity-enhancing technologies, such as artificial intelligence, process automation, data analytics and systems integration'. Investment is concentrated in hardware and customer-facing functions.
Tech adoption barriers: high implementation costs 44%, lack of internal expertise 33%.

Bukku RM0 free plan. SQL Account RM79/month. AutoCount RM2,800 one-time licence. QuickBooks RM91/month. Financio RM50/month. Xero, QuickBooks and Zoho rely on partners for e-invoicing. SQL 'inventory is not its main strength'.
The Digital Ministry worked with the Finance Ministry to settle outstanding GDPM claims. RM19 million was credited via BSN after payment delays.
38,804 PMKS (SMEs) entered digitalisation through the grant 'last year', worth RM89.6 million. Recipients must add funds equal to the grant amount.
Grant matches 50% or up to RM5,000. Applicants should deal only with approved-panel technology companies.

pains.frequency: Unknown (structural barrier, not a recurring event).
pains.money_impact: Software RM50-RM2,800 depending on product (vendor list). Grant co-funding is required. Grant payouts to vendors were delayed until May 2026.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: None directly. The consequence is that back-office work stays manual.
pains.already_spending: Yes. Subscriptions, co-funded grant purchases and RM89.6m in grants to 38,804 firms (RTM).

pains.title: SST compliance after the July 2025 expansion carries escalating late penalties
pains.description: The service tax scope widened from 1 July 2025: 8% on rental/leasing, with a RM1M registration threshold for rental and financial services. Customs waived penalties for late registration and late returns until 31 Dec 2025. Advisory sources report late-payment penalties of 10% for the first 30 days, then 15% and another 15%, up to 40% of tax due. The SME Association is still asking for SST relief 'particularly for micro and small enterprises' in October 2026. This mainly hits small firms above registration thresholds, and micro firms indirectly through SST on commercial rent. All penalty details come from advisory or vendor summaries, not RMCD primary documents.
pains.who: Small service businesses above the SST registration thresholds. Micro and small tenants paying SST on commercial rent.

evidence.what_it_says: SST scope expanded from 1 July 2025. Rental/leasing taxed at 8%, with registration once taxable services reach RM1,000,000 a year.

evidence.source: SME Association of Malaysia, Budget 2027 commentary
evidence.what_it_says: Cites cumulative increases in SST and compliance expenses. Seeks temporary SST relief on commercial rental 'particularly for micro and small enterprises'. Calls for a cumulative SME regulatory impact assessment.
Late SST filing: RM200 up to RM20,000 per offence. Errors in SST registration: up to RM20,000 per offence.
Describes the revised SST scope with new taxable items and service sectors from July 2025.

pains.frequency: Unknown. The filing cycle was not verified in the sources I read.
pains.money_impact: Late-payment penalties reported up to 40% of tax due (advisory sources). 8% SST on commercial rent where the landlord is registered.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Penalty relief ended 31 Dec 2025. Penalties enforced from 1 Jan 2026 per a vendor guide (not verified with RMCD).
pains.already_spending: Tax agents and accountants (see bookkeeping pain). Exact spend unknown.

pains.title: B2B customers pay late: 64-day average delays leave small traders, wholesalers and service vendors short of cash
pains.description: Small B2B sellers (traders, wholesalers, printers, small manufacturers, B2B service firms) give credit terms, usually 30 days, but get paid about two months late. Experian's trade data shows SMEs pay later than large firms. Most SMEs have thin cash buffers. Chasing payments is manual work: WhatsApp reminders, statements and calls. Malaysian law sets no statutory late-payment interest, so the only leverage is what the contract says or a costly legal route. Small claims are capped at RM5,000, and above that a lawyer is needed.
pains.who: Owners and finance/admin staff of micro and small B2B sellers (wholesale, trading, printing, small manufacturing, logistics, B2B services). The Experian data covers 'SMEs' as one group, so the figures are not split by micro or small.
pains.frequency: Weekly or more. Every invoice on credit terms needs tracking and follow-up. The regional Funding Societies survey (2023) found that following up on late payments was the most widespread receivables issue.
pains.money_impact: SME payment delays averaged 64 days in early 2025, against 58 days for large corporations (Experian, 21 May 2025). Transport/logistics averaged 76 days. In Q1 2025 the SME-versus-corporate gap was 26 days in transport/logistics, 13 days in hospitality and 10 days in wholesale. 70% of SMEs have less than six months of cash reserves (SAMENTA/Ipsos, Sept 2025). 42% of SMEs cite managing cash flow as a key pressure (Airwallex survey, 2026). A vendor claim that late payments cost SMEs 3-7% of margin (Capsphere) has no named source and is not used.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Malaysia has no statutory late-payment interest regime (Allianz Trade, seen in a search result only), so interest applies only if the contract says so. Small claims are capped at RM5,000, reportedly for individuals only, and take 3-4 months. Above RM5,000 a lawyer is required. Late collection also pushes the seller's own deadlines (supplier payments, payroll, EPF by the 15th) into risk.
pains.already_spending: Staff and owner hours spent chasing. Lawyers' letters of demand and legal proceedings (DNH, Low & Partners guides). Some firms use P2P or invoice financing (Capsphere, Funding Societies), which costs interest. No RM figure was verified for collection spend.

evidence.source: Experian Malaysia, State of Credit 2025 press release
evidence.what_it_says: 'payment delays across all enterprises fell from 64 days to 61 days over four years'. SMEs went 'from 69 days in 2022 to 64 days in early 2025'. Large corporations are 'averaging 58 days'. Sector gaps in 1Q 2025: 'Transport/Logistics (26 days), Hospitality (13 days), and Wholesale (10 days)'. Transport/logistics delays 'average 76 days'. The CEO said 'many SMEs remain highly exposed to cash flow gaps'. There is no micro/small split.
Repeats the Experian figures: SMEs at 64 days, large corporations at 58 days, and SME-corporate payment lags of 26 days in transport/logistics, 13 in hospitality and 10 in wholesale in Q1 2025.

evidence.source: Experian State of Credit 2025 Report (PDF). Seen only as a search-result excerpt; the PDF text could not be extracted.
evidence.what_it_says: Search excerpt: construction 'Delays decreased from 87 days in Q1 2024 to 76 days by the end of the year.' This was not verified in the PDF body.

evidence.source: Focus Malaysia on the SAMENTA SME Outlook Survey 2025/26 (Ipsos)
evidence.what_it_says: 'Seven in ten SMEs have less than six months' cash reserves.' Top challenges: inflation 40%, weak demand 33%, regulatory pressures 26%. Sample size not stated.

evidence.source: The Star on the Airwallex SME survey (by Vase.ai, 415 Malaysian SMEs, H1 2026)
evidence.what_it_says: 67% cite rising costs, 43% manpower and 42% 'managing local and global cash flow' as key pressures. 44% cite high implementation costs as a barrier to technology. Vendor-commissioned survey with no micro/small split.

evidence.source: Funding Societies. REGIONAL survey of almost 1,000 SMEs in ID, MY, SG, TH, VN.
evidence.what_it_says: Following up on late payments was the most widespread receivables issue in the region. Manual reminders lead to neglected follow-ups. Cash and cheques still dominate in Malaysia. It also cites a Coface APAC study: average delay rose from 54 days in 2021 to 67 days in 2022.
Small claims are for a 'debt of RM 5,000.00 or less' and 'may be completed within the timeline of 3 to 4 months'. A company cannot self-represent.

pains.title: Construction subcontractors: progress claims go unpaid ('pay-when-paid'), and CIPAA recovery is deadline-heavy paperwork
pains.description: Small contractors and subcontractors (M&E, renovation, specialist trades) bill progress claims and are paid late or not at all. The main causes found are clients withholding payment and main contractors applying 'pay-when-paid'. CIPAA 2012 offers fast adjudication, but only through strict written steps: a payment claim with prescribed content, a 10-working-day response window, a notice of adjudication, and a series of 10- and 5-working-day submissions. The adjudicator then has 45 working days to decide. A small firm that misses steps or lacks documents (variation orders, delivery records, WhatsApp instructions) loses leverage. AIAC CIPAA registrations reached 626 in 2024, against 29 in 2014.
pains.who: Micro and small contractors and subcontractors. SMEs are an estimated 70% of Malaysia's construction sector (MCMEA seminar, Jan 2026).
pains.frequency: Recurs with each progress claim on every project. The monthly cadence is typical industry practice but is not stated in the sources found. CIPAA deadlines are counted in working days and run in parallel across claims.
pains.money_impact: Planning Malaysia (2020): late payment 'causes severe cash flow problems to subcontractor(s)' and 'some companies have to close down their services'. Experian (search excerpt): construction payment delays went from 87 days in Q1 2024 to 76 days by end-2024. Historic project-level losses: LRT3 contractors owed more than RM700 million (2021); the DASH subcontractor consortium stood to lose RM100m (2021). These are large-project examples, not micro firms.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Payment response within 10 working days. If none is served, the non-paying party is 'deemed to have disputed the entire payment claim'. Adjudication submissions are due in 10 and 5 working days, and the decision in 45 working days. If an adjudicated sum is unpaid 14 calendar days after the decision, the winning party can give notice and then suspend or slow work after another 14 days (s.29).
pains.already_spending: AIAC adjudicator fees: RM3,036 for disputes of RM50,000 and below, RM6,336 for RM50,001-150,000, excluding taxes. Lawyers and claims consultants. Parties are jointly and severally liable for adjudication costs.

evidence.source: SCC Online report on the AIAC Asia ADR Week 2026 panel
evidence.what_it_says: 'when CIPAA came into effect in 2014, AIAC recorded 29 cases. By 2024, the number had increased to 626.' Also cites the 45-working-day decision period and enforcement hurdles (stay and setting-aside applications, winding-up petitions), described only qualitatively.

The payment response must be served within 10 working days. If none is served, the party 'is deemed to have disputed the entire payment claim'. Adjudication claim, response and reply are due in 10, 10 and 5 working days. The decision is due 'within 45 working days'. Under s.29, after 14 calendar days unpaid plus a 14-day notice, the winner may suspend or slow work.
'50,000 and below' RM3,036. '50,001 to 150,000' RM6,336. '150,001 to 300,000' RM7,796 plus 2.7% of the excess. Fees 'shall exclude all taxes'.

evidence.source: Planning Malaysia Journal, 'Late Payment Issues of Subcontractors in Malaysian Construction Industry'
evidence.what_it_says: Survey of 37 main contractors and subcontractors in Gombak, Selangor. Causes: the client withholding payment and the 'pay when paid' term. Effects: 'severe cash flow problems to subcontractor(s)'; 'some companies have to close down their services'. Small sample.

evidence.source: Malaysia SME, report of an MCMEA seminar
evidence.what_it_says: SMEs 'made up an estimated 70% of Malaysia's construction sector' and 'bore the brunt' of payment losses.

pains.title: Retention money (5-10% of contract value) stuck for months and lost when the main contractor fails
pains.description: Main contractors hold back 5-10% of each subcontract as retention. It is released in halves, at completion and after the defects liability period. A small subcontractor has to track release dates per project and chase them. A 2019 Federal Court ruling holds that retention is not trust money unless the contract says so. CIPAA does not protect retention on insolvency, so a main contractor's failure wipes it out.
pains.who: Small M&E, renovation and specialist subcontractors.
pains.frequency: Per project, with two release milestones each, so a firm running several projects has release dates every few months. The exact frequency is unknown from the sources.
pains.money_impact: Retention is 'typically 5% to 10% of a contract's value' and 'often equivalent to several months of operating cash flow' (MCMEA seminar, Jan 2026). No aggregate RM figure for lost retention was found.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Release is tied to completion and defects-liability dates in the contract. If the main contractor becomes insolvent first, the money is usually lost, since it is not held on trust unless the contract says so.
pains.already_spending: Legal advice and litigation over retention. The seminar itself (MCMEA) shows trade associations spending effort lobbying for reform. No RM figure.

evidence.source: Malaysia SME, report of a Malaysia Council of M&E Associations seminar
evidence.what_it_says: Retention sums are 'typically 5% to 10% of a contract's value'. The money is 'earned income' and 'often equivalent to several months of operating cash flow'. When it is delayed or lost, 'subcontractors faced immediate financial distress'. CIPAA 'does not protect retention sums when insolvency occurs'. Trust-account reform is still only a proposal.

evidence.source: DNH law firm, case spotlight (seen as a search result)
evidence.what_it_says: For retention to be trust money there must be clear contractual language and the sums must be separated into a trust account. A trust cannot be implied without an express clause.

pains.title: GP and panel clinics: TPA reimbursements take months, with fee cuts and onboarding fees
pains.description: Small private GP clinics treat corporate panel patients and then claim from third-party administrators (TPAs). Doctors' associations report reimbursement cycles that stretch for months. They also report part-payments in instalments, deductions of up to 10% of GP fees, and onboarding fees of up to RM5,000 to join panels. Clinics must reconcile claims against payments across several TPAs by hand. Medical associations say the problem has persisted for nearly 20 years.
pains.who: Micro and small private GP clinics, typically owner-doctor plus a few staff.
pains.frequency: Every panel patient visit generates a claim, so daily. Reconciliation and chasing happen per TPA cycle, monthly or longer.
pains.money_impact: TPAs reportedly slice off 'as much as 10 per cent of GP total fees per patient visit' and charge 'onboarding fees of up to RM5,000' (Nov 2025). Older reports (2019): TPAs charge RM2-RM5 per patient as a panel fee and set consultation fees at RM10-RM15. One doctor had RM24,000 in unpaid claims after two TPAs collapsed. In 2014, a TPA owed doctors more than RM1 million in total.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: No statutory deadline for TPAs was found. The forced consequence is cash tied up for months and the risk of total loss if a TPA collapses.
pains.already_spending: Panel and onboarding fees of up to RM5,000. Per-patient TPA deductions. Clinic staff time on claims submission and follow-up, not quantified.

evidence.source: CodeBlue, statement by FPMPAM (Federation of Private Medical Practitioners' Associations Malaysia)
evidence.what_it_says: Cites 'chronic delays in reimbursement to clinics, with payment cycles stretching for months'. GP clinics are treated as 'unwilling creditors, buffers for cashflow, and unpaid financiers of TPA operations'. Onboarding fees are 'reportedly reaching as high as RM5,000'. Concerns have persisted for 'nearly two decades'.

evidence.source: CodeBlue op-ed by the founding president of the Association of Private Practitioners Sabah
evidence.what_it_says: TPAs have 'protracted payment cycles, often taking months to reimburse clinics'. They are 'slicing off as much as 10 per cent of GP total fees per patient visit' and 'demand onboarding fees of up to RM5,000'. Clinics are paid incompletely through 'adjustments and discrepancy deductions'.

'TPAs charge RM2 to RM5 per patient as the panel fee'. Consultation fees are set 'between RM10 and RM15'. Payments come in stages ('Sometimes, you get RM120, and the next time, you get RM400'). One doctor had unpaid claims of 'RM24,000'. The article is older.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (seen as a search result)
evidence.what_it_says: Doctors said TPA Medijaring owed more than RM1 million. One Sitiawan doctor was still waiting for RM15,657 for services in 2011-2012. Old, but shows the long-running pattern.

pains.title: Appointment no-shows in clinics, dental practices and salons waste paid capacity daily
pains.description: Appointment businesses take bookings by WhatsApp and phone, and a missed slot cannot be resold. The only rigorous Malaysian no-show rates found come from public or teaching settings, not private SMEs. Hospital Kuala Lumpur outpatient clinics had a 28% no-show rate. A dental student clinic at USIM had 37.1% missed appointments. A paediatric dental audit found 45.8% defaulting, falling to 26.9% after phone reminders. Private-SME figures come only from vendors and are unsourced.
pains.who: Micro and small private clinics (GP, dental, aesthetic), salons, spas, physiotherapy and tuition or class-based businesses.
pains.frequency: Daily.
pains.money_impact: Vendor estimate, with no source or method: one peak-hour GP no-show costs RM200-RM500. Its example of 15% no-shows on 40 daily appointments works out to about RM24,000-RM60,000 a month. Treat this as illustrative. No independent Malaysian RM figure was found.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: The slot is lost permanently. The forced consequence is idle staff and chair time.
pains.already_spending: Staff time on manual reminder calls and WhatsApp messages (the phone-reminder intervention in the dental audit). Paid booking and reminder tools are marketed heavily in Malaysia. A vendor gives WhatsApp utility messages at about RM0.05 each (unverified LinkedIn vendor post).

evidence.source: Machine Learning Predictions on Outpatient No-Show Appointments in a Malaysia Major Tertiary Hospital. Seen as a search result; the full text was blocked by a browser check.
evidence.date: Data from 2019; publication date not verified
evidence.what_it_says: Search excerpt: Hospital Kuala Lumpur outpatient clinics, 246,943 appointment records, 28% no-show rate. Public hospital, not an SME.

evidence.source: USIM dental clinic study. Seen as a search result; the page failed to load.
evidence.what_it_says: Search excerpt: 202 patient folders, missed-appointment rate 37.1% (95% CI 30.7-44.0). Teaching clinic, not an SME.

evidence.source: Malaysian Journal of Medicine supplement, clinical audit at Hospital Taiping. Seen as a search result; PDF text unreadable.
evidence.what_it_says: Search excerpt: first-cycle defaulter rate 45.8%, falling to 26.9% after telephone reminders (not significant per the authors). Public hospital.

'a single no-show during peak hours means RM200 to RM500 in lost revenue' for a typical GP clinic. Its example: 'A clinic with a 15% no-show rate and 40 daily appointments loses the equivalent of six consultations per day.' No source or method is given.

evidence.source: Bernama on the Meta and KUSKOP Small Business Growth Academy
evidence.what_it_says: Meta research: 'eight in 10 Malaysians prefer messaging to reach a business'. MSMEs 'make up 97 per cent of our businesses' (KUSKOP minister). This supports WhatsApp being the booking channel.

pains.title: WhatsApp enquiries and quotations not answered or followed up in time, so the job goes to a competitor
pains.description: Malaysian customers prefer to message businesses, so enquiries, quote requests and order changes arrive on the owner's personal or shared WhatsApp. Small teams miss messages or answer late, and quotes are not followed up. Buyers who message several suppliers go with the first reply. Malaysia-specific evidence of lost revenue is thin: only vendor case studies and unsourced claims were found. This is a plausible pain without independent proof.
pains.who: Micro and small service firms (aircon, cleaning, renovation, events, printing, workshops) and B2B traders who quote on request.
pains.frequency: Daily. One Malaysian motorbike dealer's team handled 500-600 messages a day (vendor case study).
pains.money_impact: Unknown, with no independent Malaysian figure. The widely repeated claim that '78% of buyers choose the first responder' traces to InsideSales.com B2B data via vendor blogs and could not be verified. A Campaign Asia headline says '97% of APAC businesses fail on response time to online leads', but the method is paywalled.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: There is no formal deadline. The forced consequence is losing the lead to a faster competitor.
pains.already_spending: Owners' and staff time. Some firms pay for WhatsApp CRM and AI-agent tools (respond.io customers in Malaysia). No RM spend figure was found.

evidence.what_it_says: 'eight in 10 Malaysians prefer messaging to reach a business' (Meta research).

evidence.source: respond.io, a VENDOR blog with its own case studies
evidence.what_it_says: iMotorbike (Malaysia/Vietnam) agents were 'struggling with 500 to 600 messages a day'. After AI agents, they reply '67% faster'. A Malaysian beauty group's 'Appointments booked over chat rose 18x'. The 'buyer ... can message three businesses in a minute and buy from the first one that answers' line is illustrative, not data.
Headline only: '97% of APAC businesses fail on response time to online leads'. Businesses are losing 'potentially millions'. Method not visible.

pains.title: E-invoicing (MyInvois) per-transaction compliance for small B2B sellers above the exemption threshold
pains.description: Small B2B traders, wholesalers, printers and manufacturers above the exemption line must issue LHDN e-invoices. During the relaxation period they may consolidate monthly. But any single transaction above RM10,000 needs its own e-invoice, which hits B2B traders with large orders. Phase 4 (RM1-5 million turnover) started on 1 January 2026. The exemption threshold has moved several times. RM500,000 is officially confirmed (June 2025). RM1 million and RM3 million appear only in secondary sources and were not verified. Most micro firms are likely exempt; small firms near the line face uncertainty.
pains.who: Small B2B sellers with annual turnover above the exemption threshold (officially RM500k as of June 2025; possibly RM1m or RM3m since, unverified). Micro firms are mostly exempt.
pains.frequency: Per transaction for sales above RM10,000; monthly consolidation for the rest.
pains.money_impact: Software, accountant and setup costs. No verified RM figure for micro and small firms. 44% of SMEs cite high implementation costs as a technology barrier (Airwallex survey, 2026, not specific to e-invoicing).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Under Income Tax Act s.120(1)(d): a fine of RM200-RM20,000, up to 6 months' imprisonment, or both, per non-compliance (beancount.io, a secondary source). LHDN said no prosecution during the grace period if consolidated e-invoice rules are followed. A secondary source says the relaxation period was extended to 31 Dec 2027 (unverified against LHDN).
pains.already_spending: Accounting software subscriptions and accountants; amounts unknown.

evidence.what_it_says: Businesses 'below RM500,000 are exempted'. Phase 4 (above RM1m to RM5m) begins Jan 1, 2026. Phase 5 (up to RM1m) postponed to July 1, 2026. 'no prosecution will be initiated under Section 120' during the grace period. Every sale or service above RM10,000 needs an individual e-invoice.

Claims the exemption threshold rose to RM3 million 'effective September 1, 2026', freeing about 1.1 million MSMEs, and that relaxation runs to December 31, 2027. Penalty RM200-RM20,000 and/or up to 6 months per non-compliance. Transactions over RM10,000 need an individual e-invoice. NOT confirmed by an official LHDN source.

pains.title: Monthly statutory payroll deadlines (EPF by the 15th) with heavy enforcement
pains.description: Every employer must remit EPF (and SOCSO/EIS) by the 15th of the following month. For micro employers, payroll and contributions are often done by the owner or an outsourced accountant. When customers pay late, this deadline gets squeezed. EPF enforcement in 2025 was large-scale. The enforcement data does not separate micro firms, and it does not show whether defaults come from admin slips or from cash shortfalls.
pains.who: All micro and small employers, including service businesses and small manufacturers.
pains.frequency: Monthly.
pains.money_impact: Unknown for micro firms. 2014 data showed individual fines of RM4,000-RM6,000 (144 employers fined, RM200,000 in total). That is old.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Contributions are due 'on or before the 15th of the following month'. In 2025 EPF filed 3,530 civil suits and took 6,011 criminal actions. 14,332 company directors were barred from overseas travel as of Dec 2025, with 2,257 new names in 2025 (from a search-result excerpt of The Sun; the page itself returned 403).
pains.already_spending: Outsourced payroll and accountant fees, amount unknown.

evidence.what_it_says: Search excerpt: in 2025 EPF filed 3,530 civil suits and took 6,011 criminal actions against employers and directors. 14,332 directors are barred from leaving Malaysia as of December 2025, after 2,257 new names in 2025.
Employers must remit 'on or before the 15th of the following month'. 144 employers were fined, with fines 'in the range of RM4000 to RM6000' (Jul-Sep 2014). Old data.

services-b2b.context_notes:
ORBYTE PROFILE: No source on Orbyte or Alpha Red Solutions was searched in this run. The other research angles should cover that.

MARKET CONTEXT:
- MSMEs are '97 per cent of our businesses and nearly half of our workforce' (KUSKOP minister, Bernama, 26 Sept 2026).
- 8 in 10 Malaysians prefer messaging to reach a business (Meta via Bernama, 26 Sept 2026). This supports WhatsApp as the default channel for bookings, quotes and orders.
- Meta and KUSKOP launched a 'Small Business Growth Academy' for WhatsApp Business and AI tools (Sept 2026). Big players are already targeting MSME WhatsApp workflows, so differentiation matters.

STRONGEST MALAYSIA-SPECIFIC SIGNALS (for the orchestrator):
- (a) Receivables and late payment. Experian 2025: SMEs 64 days vs corporates 58. SAMENTA 2025: 70% have under 6 months of cash.
- (b) Construction payment chain. CIPAA statutory working-day deadlines, 626 AIAC cases in 2024, retention of 5-10%, SMEs about 70% of construction.
- (c) GP clinic receivables from TPAs. 2025 association complaints about delays of months, deductions of up to 10% and onboarding fees of up to RM5,000.
All three are 'money stuck plus manual chasing plus a deadline'. They fit the super-pain bar better than no-shows or lead response, whose Malaysian evidence is vendor-heavy.

POLICY FACTS CHECKED:
- SST expansion on 1 July 2025: beauty services (manicure, facials, hairdressing) were REMOVED from scope on 27 June 2025 (FMT, The Sun). Salons do NOT face new service tax. Construction, private healthcare and education stayed in scope. Rental and financial-services thresholds were raised to RM1m.
- Minimum wage RM1,700 applied to all employers from 1 Aug 2025. An Oct 2026 report says the government moves to RM2,000 from June 2027, with an exemption for MSMEs under RM50m sales. This is from a search result and was not verified against an official source.
- E-invoicing: the officially confirmed exemption is under RM500k (LHDN, June 2025). RM1m (Dec 2025) and RM3m (Sept 2026) appear only in blogs and forums. Verify on the MyInvois/LHDN site before using.
- No Malaysian late-payment statute or 'Prompt Payment Act' was found. Allianz Trade (search result) says the law gives no late-payment framework, so interest must be contractual.

pains.title: Exempt from e-invoicing on paper, but big customers still demand e-invoices or TINs and hold back payment
pains.description: Since 1 Sep 2026, businesses with annual turnover below RM3 million are exempt from MyInvois e-invoicing. Most micro and small firms are now outside the mandate. But SME associations report that larger customers who already use e-invoicing still ask exempt suppliers for TINs and e-invoices. Some customers delay or hold back payment when a supplier issues a conventional invoice. Different procurement and accounting processes at each large customer add confusion. Some businesses also still believe expenses cannot be claimed without an LHDN-validated e-invoice. The painful prep work: knowing which customer needs which document, keeping TIN, SSM, SST and buyer details ready, showing evidence of exempt status, and chasing invoices stuck in a customer's AP queue. Exemption is also not automatic. A small firm is caught through its group if a corporate shareholder, holding company, related company or JV partner has RM3 million or more in turnover, so status must be re-checked every year.
pains.who: Micro and small B2B suppliers (below RM3m turnover) selling to medium or large companies: trading, contractors, services, logistics, F&B suppliers
pains.frequency: Every B2B invoice to a large customer: weekly or more for active suppliers
pains.money_impact: Cash stuck: payments 'delayed simply because they are not issuing e-invoices' (SME Association of Malaysia, Sep 2026). No source quantifies the RM amount.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Commercial, not statutory: customers withhold or delay payment. LHDN does not require exempt firms to issue e-invoices.
pains.already_spending: Some firms prepared early and are 'spending on accounting systems, software integration'. Christine Koh says some 'may now find themselves exempt after already incurring these costs' (The Star, 4 Sep 2026).

evidence.what_it_says: Chin Chee Seong (SME Association of Malaysia) warns against exempt SMEs 'being asked to comply with additional requirements that are not required by LHDN' or 'their payments being delayed simply because they are not issuing e-invoices'. William Ng (Samenta) says larger clients 'were actively asking some exempt suppliers for information such as their Tax Identification Number' and that 'payments should not be withheld'. Ng also says 'Some businesses still believed they could not substantiate expenses for tax purposes without an LHDN-validated e-invoice'. Christine Koh says the threshold moved 'from RM150,000 to RM500,000, RM1mil and now RM3mil'.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (from the search-result summary; the full text returned 403)
evidence.what_it_says: Headline: 'Higher threshold, same headache: SMEs push for simpler tax reporting'. The SME Association of Malaysia says exempted firms still face practical problems, including possible payment delays when major corporations impose extra requirements. The threshold exempts 'more than 1.1 million businesses' per IRB.

evidence.source: LHDN/HASiL official e-Invoice implementation timeline (last updated 30/08/2026)
evidence.what_it_says: 'Taxpayers with an annual turnover or revenue of less than RM3,000,000 are exempted from e-Invoice implementation.'

The threshold was raised 'from RM1 million to RM3 million in annual revenue or sales', effective 1 September 2026. The change also affects buyers from local suppliers, because suppliers below the threshold may issue non-electronic invoices.

evidence.source: GRITC (accounting firm blog, cites LHDN Guideline v4.8)
evidence.what_it_says: Exemption announced 30 Aug 2026, effective 1 Sep 2026. It does not apply where a non-individual shareholder, holding company, related company or JV partner has revenue of RM3m or more.

pains.title: Small firms between RM3m and RM5m (or in a larger group) must run monthly e-invoice consolidation and individual e-invoices for every transaction above RM10,000
pains.description: Phase 4 (turnover up to RM5m) started 1 Jan 2026. After the new exemption, it covers RM3m–RM5m firms, plus smaller firms caught by the group test. During the relaxation period to 31 Dec 2027, they may issue monthly consolidated e-invoices. These must reach MyInvois within 7 calendar days after month end. From 1 Jan 2026, any single transaction above RM10,000 needs its own e-invoice and cannot be consolidated. Full per-transaction enforcement is reported to start 1 Jan 2028. The painful prep work: collecting buyer TIN/ID details, flagging transactions above RM10,000 as they happen, and getting the month's sales data into shape within 7 days. Owners or teams of 2 or fewer usually do this work. Survey: 55% of SMEs lack a clear understanding of the requirements, and smaller SMEs cite lack of time.
pains.who: Small firms with RM3m–RM5m turnover. Also below-RM3m firms with a corporate shareholder or related company at RM3m or more. Note: a 5–30 staff services or trading firm can easily reach RM3m.
pains.frequency: Monthly (consolidation within 7 days of month end) plus every transaction above RM10,000
pains.money_impact: Penalties per offence (below). Spending on systems and integration. No source quantifies lost revenue.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Consolidated e-invoice within 7 calendar days after month end. Section 120(1)(d) ITA 1967: 'a fine of RM200 to RM20,000, imprisonment of up to six months, or both, for each offence'. LHDN does not prosecute during relaxation if monthly consolidated e-invoices are issued.
pains.already_spending: Accounting systems, software integration (The Star, Sep 2026). Smaller SMEs rely on owners or lean teams of two or fewer (Xero, May 2025).

evidence.source: GRITC (cites LHDN Guideline v4.8 and Specific Guideline v4.9)
evidence.what_it_says: Phase 4: 1 Jan 2026, 'in practice RM3 million to RM5 million after the new exemption'. Concessionary date 1 July 2026 for some businesses. Relaxation period 'runs until 31 December 2027'. 'any single transaction above RM10,000 must have its own individual e-Invoice'. Penalty: 'a fine of RM200 to RM20,000, imprisonment of up to six months, or both, for each offence'.

Consolidated e-invoices 'must reach MyInvois within 7 calendar days after the end of the month they cover'. The RM10,000 rule is not suspended during relaxation. Full enforcement from 1 Jan 2028. 'Treat "exempt today" as a status to re-check each year'.
Phase 4 relaxation 'stretches all the way to 31 December 2027'. Consolidated e-invoices are allowed, B2B included. 'No penalties apply under Section 120' during relaxation.

Top challenges: unclear requirements 55%, digitising large volumes of data 49%, data security 47%, limited in-house technical capability 45%. Confidence: 57% of smaller SMEs vs 65% of larger. Smaller businesses rely on owners or teams of two or fewer and cite lack of time.

ACCCIM notes consolidated e-invoicing is not allowed once a single transaction reaches RM10,000. It asks to align that limit with AML cash reporting levels (RM25,000 general) and calls for SME-friendly e-invoicing.

pains.title: SST: tracking registration thresholds, filing bi-monthly returns (even nil), and the new rental service tax on business premises
pains.description: SST scope expanded on 1 July 2025. The registration threshold is RM500,000 for most newly taxable services and RM1m for rental/leasing and fee-based financial services. A Sarawak SME leader cites RM1.5m for F&B, construction and private healthcare. Businesses must test turnover on backward- and forward-looking 12-month rules, and sources say this rule confuses businesses. Once registered, SST-02 is due every two months by the last day of the following month, and a nil return is still mandatory. Rental service tax was 8% from 1 Jul to 31 Dec 2025 and 6% from 1 Jan 2026, per a secondary source. Recovered utility charges count as taxable rent. The Customs Rental & Leasing Guide 2nd Edition (14 May 2026, per a law-firm summary) adds an SME tenant exemption. Tenants must register through the MyPMK system to claim it, so an SME that does not register may pay tax on its shop or office rent. The painful prep work: rolling 12-month turnover watch per service code, classifying services (for example marketing vs advertising), assembling bi-monthly figures, and SME-tenant paperwork.
pains.who: Micro and small service providers near the thresholds; small landlords of commercial space; SME tenants of commercial premises; F&B above RM1.5m
pains.frequency: Bi-monthly returns (6 per year), with continuous threshold monitoring
pains.money_impact: Rental tax of 6% (2026) on commercial rent if the exemption is not claimed. Late payment penalties of 10% rising to a reported 40% of tax due. MOF says 1,325 traders collected SST without registering (2024 to Jan 2026). The URL slug mentions 'RM767m repaid', but the article body could not be read, so that figure's meaning is unverified.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Late payment: 10% for the first 30 days, plus 15% for each of the next two 30-day periods, maximum 40% (secondary sources). Failure to register or file: fines up to RM50,000 or up to 3 years' jail or both (secondary).
pains.already_spending: Unknown from sources. Industry groups (strata, pest control) reported 'paying under protest' amid confusing guidance (May 2025).

evidence.what_it_says: From 1 July 2025, the rental/leasing threshold rises 'from RM500,000 to RM1 million in total annual sales' at 8%, 'providing relief to more Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)'. The beauty-services expansion was dropped.
'About 75% of small and medium-sized enterprises will be exempted from the additional 8% levy', per Samenta president William Ng. The remaining 25% are still in scope.

Rental tax is 8% for 1 Jul–31 Dec 2025 and 6% from 1 Jan 2026. Group K threshold is RM1,000,000. Customs released the Rental & Leasing Services Guide (2nd Edition) on 14 May 2026. Recovered utility charges are taxable. SME tenants must 'Register through the MyPMK System' to get the rental service tax exemption.
Strata and pest-management associations asked for a pause. Members were paying 'under protest' amid confusing guidelines. Some were told registration is unnecessary and others were told to comply.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (from the search-result summary; fetch returned 403)
evidence.what_it_says: MOF: 1,325 traders collected SST without registering from 2024 to January 2026. The 'RM767m repaid' in the URL slug was not verified.

evidence.source: Borneo Post (SME Sarawak president Jordan Ong)
evidence.what_it_says: 'about 77 per cent are micro businesses', and many have 'only one or two administrative staff'. Cites SST thresholds of RM1.5 million (F&B, construction, private healthcare) and RM500,000 (accommodation, logistics, rental/leasing). Asks for 'simplified invoicing, less frequent reporting'.
SST returns are due every two months by the last day of the following month. Filing is mandatory even with no tax payable. Escalating late penalties reach a 40% cumulative cap (secondary).

pains.title: Local council (PBT) business premise and signboard licences: annual renewal, new BMW toilet rule for food premises, enforcement compounds
pains.description: Council business licences have generally been valid for one year. In Kuala Lumpur, DBKL is moving to optional 2–3 year renewals from 1 July 2026, but only for licensees with no outstanding compounds or rent arrears. Signboards need their own advertisement licence. DBKL issued 211 offence notices for advertisements without a valid licence (Jan to 16 Oct 2024) and can take signboards down. Since January 2026, food premises in 20 city-status areas will not have their business licence renewed if their toilets fail the 'BMW' standard. Reported phasing: municipal councils in 2027 and district councils in 2028. The painful prep work: knowing each licence's expiry date, clearing old compounds first, keeping premises, signboard and toilet compliance ready before inspection, and handling council-specific rules.
pains.who: Every micro or small business with a physical premise (shops, F&B, salons, workshops), especially F&B in city council areas
pains.frequency: Annual renewal (moving to 2–3 years in KL for clean licensees). Inspections and enforcement operations happen at any time.
pains.money_impact: No licence renewal means the premise cannot legally operate. Compounds apply, and signboards can be removed. Toilet upgrade costs are not quantified. IDEAS (2019) ranked company billboard regulation among the costliest rules for micro and small service firms.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Food premises failing BMW 'will not have their business licences renewed'. Compounds for unlicensed signboards (amounts not found). Multi-year renewal is blocked if any compound is outstanding.
pains.already_spending: Unknown in current sources. IDEAS (2019): only 7%–35% of payments for the most time-consuming regulations were made online; 'the rest of payments being made over the counter or outsourced'.

evidence.what_it_says: From 1 July, DBKL allows licence renewal for up to 3 years, up from one year, if the licensee has no 'kompaun atau tunggakan bayaran sewa'. Discount is 5% for 2 years and 10% for 3 years. About 95,000 licensees expected to benefit.
From January 2026, food premises in 20 city areas (restaurants, F&B outlets, cafés) 'will not have their business licences renewed if they fail to meet the BMW level'.

evidence.source: SAYS Seismik (from the search-result summary, with RTM)
evidence.what_it_says: Rollout starts with city councils in 2026, then municipal councils in 2027 and district councils in 2028.

From January to 16 October, DBKL issued 211 offence notices under UUK 5(1) for displaying advertisements without a valid licence, and 20 notices plus 10 enforcement notices on national-language signage rules.
31 offence notices at six malls, including signboards with no advertisement licence. Premises were 'dikenakan kompaun' and DBKL can remove signboards.
Samenta lists '"BMW" toilet requirements for renewing food business licences' among new compliance costs pushing SMEs into a 'survival zone'.

evidence.source: IDEAS (survey of 120 micro and small services firms, Klang Valley)
evidence.what_it_says: The most costly regulations: corporate tax, minimum wage, company billboard regulation, worker visa/permit. This source is old (2019).

pains.title: F&B: every food handler needs typhoid vaccination and food-handler training, or the premise risks closure
pains.description: Under the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009, food handlers must be vaccinated against typhoid and trained at an MOH-recognised school. MOH (Feb 2025) warned that non-compliance may lead to closure orders of up to 14 days under Section 11 of the Food Act 1983, plus fines. Enforcement is visible: Kedah's 2025 Ramadan bazaar checks found 3% of handlers unvaccinated and 10% untrained, and 112 compounds were issued. In 2024, Ramadan bazaar operations produced 1,639 notices under Section 32B, and 3 premises were ordered closed. The painful prep work: keeping each worker's vaccination and training proof on file, knowing when a new hire still lacks them, and producing the documents during a surprise inspection. No source was found on the vaccination validity period or staff turnover, so those are not claimed.
pains.who: Micro and small F&B operators: restaurants, cafés, stalls, caterers, bazaar and expo vendors
pains.frequency: Every new hire, plus surprise inspections. Seasonal enforcement peaks (Ramadan bazaars).
pains.money_impact: A closure of up to 14 days means about two weeks of lost revenue. Compounds and fines apply (amounts not verified).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Closure order of up to 14 days (s11 Food Act 1983). Fines under the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009. Compounds.
pains.already_spending: Unknown. One expert says the vaccine is free at government clinics; training cost was not found.

evidence.source: Malay Mail (from the search-result summary; fetch returned 403)
evidence.what_it_says: MOH: stall operators at fairs and expos must ensure every food handler is typhoid-vaccinated and trained at MOH-recognised schools. Non-compliance may bring closure orders of up to 14 days under Section 11 of the Food Act 1983 and fines under the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009.

evidence.source: The Sun (from the search-result summary; fetch returned 403)
evidence.what_it_says: Kedah 2025 Ramadan bazaar checks: 112 compounds. 3% of food handlers lacked typhoid vaccination and 10% had not attended mandatory food-handler training.
During the 2024 Ramadan bazaar operation, MOH issued 1,639 notices under Section 32B of the Food Act 1983, and 3 food premises were ordered closed under Section 11.

evidence.source: The Sun (from the search-result summary; date not confirmed)
evidence.what_it_says: Under the Food Hygiene Regulations 2009, enforced by MOH, typhoid vaccination is mandatory for all food handlers.

pains.title: SSM annual return and financial statements for Sdn Bhd: easy to miss, compounds of RM5,000 to RM40,000 per offence
pains.description: Every Sdn Bhd must lodge an annual return within 30 days of each incorporation anniversary. Financial statements must be circulated within 6 months of financial year end and lodged within 30 days after that. Directors often confuse the annual return date with the financial year end. Many discover overdue filings only when a bank, tender committee or investor asks for the company's SSM profile. Normal compounds: s68 annual return RM5,000; s248 financial statements RM40,000; s245 accounting records RM40,000; s258 circulation RM5,000. SSM ran a Statutory Document Lodgement Recovery Campaign (16 Apr–30 Sep 2026) that cut compounds by 90%–98.75%, which signals a sizeable backlog. No official count of defaulters was found. The painful prep work: tracking anniversary and financial-year dates, getting bookkeeping ready for the accountant and auditor, and collecting director and shareholder or beneficial-owner information.
pains.who: Micro and small firms incorporated as Sdn Bhd (not sole proprietors or partnerships)
pains.frequency: Annual. This fails the weekly bar, but the penalties are severe.
pains.money_impact: Compounds of RM5,000 to RM40,000 per offence. Conviction: 'a fine of up to RM50,000 for the company and every officer in default'. Blocks bank loans and tenders.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Annual return within 30 days of the incorporation anniversary. Compounds per Companies Act 2016 s68/245/248/258. Persistent non-compliance can lead to strike-off.
pains.already_spending: Firms pay company secretarial and accounting firms; the sources are such firms marketing these services. Fees were not found in the sources.

evidence.what_it_says: Campaign runs 16 April to 30 September 2026. Normal and reduced compounds: s68 annual return RM5,000 to RM500; s248 financial statements RM40,000 to RM500; s245 accounting records RM40,000 to RM2,000; s258 circulation RM5,000 to RM500.

Annual return due '30 days from the incorporation anniversary'. Confusing it with financial year end is the 'most common filing mistake among first-time directors'. Many directors discover overdue filings when a bank, tender committee or investor requests the SSM profile.

Annual return penalty: 'RM500 to RM50,000 SSM compound plus director liability'. Conviction: 'a fine of up to RM50,000 for the company and every officer in default'. Financial statements circulated within six months of FYE and lodged within 30 days of circulation.

evidence.source: SSM official X account (from the search-result summary)
evidence.what_it_says: The campaign started 16 April 2026 and helps companies remediate overdue statutory documents such as annual returns and financial statements.

Compound reductions of 90% to 98.75%, saving 'RM900 and RM39,500 per offence'. Companies get 3 months for overdue annual returns and beneficial ownership information and 6 months for financial statements.

pains.title: Stamp duty self-assessment from 1 Jan 2026: tenancy and lease agreements must be self-stamped within 30 days
pains.description: Since 1 Jan 2026, rental and lease instruments, general stamping and securities are under the Stamp Duty Self-Assessment System (Phase 1). The taxpayer files a return on MyTax, uploads the instrument and pays without prior LHDN adjudication. Instruments must be stamped within 30 days of signing. Late stamping costs RM50 or 10% of duty (31 days–3 months) and RM100 or 20% after 3 months. Failing to submit a return, or keeping poor records, risks a fine of up to RM10,000; an incorrect return is fined RM1,000–RM10,000. Records must be kept for 7 years, and an audit framework has applied since 1 Jan 2025. Samenta lists the self-assessment system among 2026 compliance burdens. Employment contracts have also been stampable since 2025 (Samenta: salaries above RM3,000), which overlaps with HR. The painful prep work: tracking every signed tenancy, service or supply agreement, calculating duty correctly, and keeping a 7-year evidence file.
pains.who: Micro and small firms that rent premises, lease equipment, sign service/supply contracts, or hire staff on written contracts
pains.frequency: Each new or renewed agreement (tenancies are typically renewed every 1–3 years; contracts per hire or deal). Not weekly for most micro firms.
pains.money_impact: Late penalties of RM50 or 10% to RM100 or 20%. Fines of up to RM10,000 for not filing or for record failures; RM1,000–RM10,000 for incorrect returns.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Stamp within 30 days of execution. Penalties as above (Ecovis, Jul 2025).
pains.already_spending: Unknown

evidence.what_it_says: Phase 1 from 1 January 2026: 'Instruments or agreements relating to rentals or leases, general stamping and securities'. Stamp 'within 30 days'. Late penalty 'RM50 or 10%' (31 days–3 months) and 'RM100 or 20%' (over 3 months). Not furnishing a return: 'Fine not exceeding RM10, 000'. Incorrect return: RM1,000–RM10,000. Keep records '7 years'. Stamp Duty Audit Framework effective 1 January 2025.
Samenta names the stamp duty self-assessment system (effective 1 Jan 2026) and stamp duty on employment contracts for salaries above RM3,000 as new compliance costs.
Describes the significant stamp duty changes from 2025 and the move to self-assessment.

pains.title: Overlapping statutory calendar run by owners with one or two admin staff
pains.description: This is the cross-cutting pain behind the items above. A small firm faces e-invoice status checks, SST bi-monthly returns, SSM annual return and financial statements, Form C within 7 months of year end, council licence renewal, stamp duty within 30 days, F&B health documents, and PDPA duties. Each has its own portal and date. Samenta (Jan 2026) says the 'cumulative cost of regulatory compliance reaches a breaking point'. It adds that small businesses lack the legal, ESG or IT departments 'needed to manage these overlapping regulatory timelines', and that compliance erodes net margins of 10–15%. SME Sarawak says about 77% of businesses are micro, many with 'only one or two administrative staff'. IDEAS (2019, older) found corporate tax compliance alone took 44 days of staff time. Rules also keep changing: the e-invoice threshold moved 4 times and rental SST moved from 8% to 6%. Old guides stay online and contradict current rules: a Sep 2026 accounting-firm calendar still states the RM1m e-invoice exemption.
pains.who: Owners and lean admin staff of micro and small firms, especially Sdn Bhd with physical premises
pains.frequency: Continuous: monthly or bi-monthly deadlines plus annual renewals across agencies
pains.money_impact: Compliance spending erodes 10–15% net margins (Samenta, no RM figure). Penalties stack across agencies (see the items above).
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Multiple: see the e-invoice, SST, SSM, PBT, stamp duty and F&B items
pains.already_spending: Accountants and company secretaries (implied by the sources; fees not found). IDEAS 2019: many payments 'made over the counter or outsourced'.

evidence.what_it_says: SMEs enter a 'survival zone' as 'the cumulative cost of regulatory compliance reaches a breaking point'. Lists stamp duty self-assessment, the foreign worker multi-tier levy, BMW toilets, e-invoicing, EPR, CBAM, DPOs under PDPA, OSH coordinators for SMEs with more than 5 employees, and NSRF. Says small firms lack departments 'needed to manage these overlapping regulatory timelines'. Net margins are 10–15%.

'about 77 per cent are micro businesses', and many have 'only one or two administrative staff'. Warns that added 'detailed invoices, transaction records, input-output tax reconciliation, periodic submissions' could impose significant costs.

evidence.source: IDEAS (2019, 120 micro and small service firms, Klang Valley)
evidence.what_it_says: Corporate tax compliance took '44 days of staff time'. Online payment for the most time-consuming regulations was 7%–35%; the rest was over the counter or outsourced.

2026 Sdn Bhd calendar: Form C 'within seven months after the accounting period ends', SST bi-monthly 'six filing cycles a year', Form E by 31 March 2026, SSM annual return. It still says companies 'below RM1 million are described as exempt' from e-invoicing, which is outdated after 1 Sep 2026.

pains.title: PDPA amendments: 72-hour breach notification for all data controllers; DPO required above data-volume triggers
pains.description: Since 1 June 2025, data controllers must notify the PDP Commissioner of a breach that causes or may cause 'significant harm' 'as soon as practicable and within 72 hours'. Affected individuals must be told within 7 days of notifying the Commissioner. A breach register must be kept for at least 2 years. A DPO is mandatory when processing personal data of more than 20,000 data subjects, sensitive data including financial information of more than 10,000, or when activities involve regular and systematic monitoring. The Commissioner must be notified of the DPO within 21 days. No size-based SME exemption was found. The maximum fine for breaching the PDP Principles rose from RM300,000 to RM1,000,000. Most micro firms will be below the DPO triggers. The breach duty still applies, and customer lists sit in WhatsApp and spreadsheets. Clinics, tuition centres or firms holding financial data may cross the 10,000 sensitive-data trigger.
pains.who: All data controllers; DPO duty only above the thresholds (likelier for clinics, education, retail loyalty lists, small fintech or insurance agencies)
pains.frequency: Event-driven (breach). DPO is a one-off appointment plus ongoing upkeep. Does not meet the weekly bar.
pains.money_impact: Fine of up to RM1,000,000 and/or up to 3 years for PDP Principle breaches (amended). Specific fines for failure to notify were not verified.
pains.deadline_or_penalty: 72 hours to notify the Commissioner; 7 days after that to notify data subjects; 21 days to notify of the DPO appointment
pains.already_spending: Unknown. Samenta lists DPOs among new SME compliance costs (Jan 2026).

evidence.what_it_says: In force 1 June 2025. DPO triggers: 'more than 20,000 data subjects', sensitive incl. financial 'more than 10,000', 'regular and systematic monitoring'. Notify DPO 'within 21 days'. Breach: Commissioner 'within 72 hours'; data subjects 'within seven days of notifying the Commissioner'. Breach register 'for at least two years'.
'Every data controller and data processor must appoint one or more DPO(s)' in the listed scenarios. Mentions no size-based exemption. Sections 12A/12B in force 1 June 2025.
The amendment raises the maximum penalty for breaching the PDP Principles from RM300,000 / 2 years to RM1,000,000 / 3 years.

pains.title: Halal certification and renewal: premises upgrades and slow approvals hit micro and small food producers (weak, older evidence)
pains.description: In 2023 the Deputy PM acknowledged that applications from micro, small and medium enterprises (PMKS) had problems meeting JAKIM conditions, especially upgrading production premises, which 'may be quite expensive'. He cited complaints that approvals took 'between nine months and two years', and a 23-working-day target was set. Later reports mention a 15-working-day trial (date unclear) and, under Budget 2025, 100 more halal auditors plus about RM600m in halal SME financing. No 2025–2026 source on renewal pain, fees or halal-executive staffing rules for micro firms was found. The painful prep work (inferred, not evidenced): keeping supplier halal certificates and ingredient records current before renewal.
pains.who: Micro and small food and beverage manufacturers and F&B outlets seeking or renewing JAKIM/state halal certification
pains.frequency: Periodic renewal (interval not verified in sources)
pains.money_impact: Premises modification costs ('may be quite expensive'), not quantified
pains.deadline_or_penalty: Unknown from sources. Certificates can be revoked for non-compliance (counts not verified).
pains.already_spending: Unknown

compliance.context_notes:
E-INVOICE STATUS (verified on the official LHDN page, last updated 30/08/2026): the exemption is turnover below RM3,000,000. Phase 4 ('up to RM5 million') started 1 Jan 2026. The PM announced the RM3m threshold on 30 Aug 2026 in his National Day address, effective 1 Sep (RTM, KPMG). Over 1.1 million businesses are reported exempt. Relaxation for Phase 4 runs to 31 Dec 2027 per secondary sources (ClearTax, GRITC, Beancount); the official timeline page does not state it. The threshold history is RM150k, RM500k (Jul 2024), RM1m (Dec 2025), RM3m (Sep 2026). Many guides online are now outdated: 3ecpa (Sep 2026) still cites RM1m, and sharedserviceslink claims a delay to Jan 2027. For Orbyte this means statutory e-invoicing is mostly NOT a pain for micro firms any more. The live pain is (a) customer pressure on exempt suppliers and (b) the RM3m–RM5m band plus group-test firms. The official LHDN media release PDF (hasil.gov.my/wp-content/uploads/20260830-Kenyataan-Media-HASiL_AMBANG-PENGECUALIAN-E_INVOIS-DINAIKKAN.pdf) was fetched but its text could not be extracted.

BUDGET 2027 (tabled 9 Oct 2026): no hybrid SST-GST model announced (Deloitte). SME income tax cut: first RM150k from 15% to 14%, and RM150,001–RM600,000 from 17% to 16%. No new SME compliance-relief measure was found. ACCCIM had asked for rental SST on MSMEs to go from 6% to 4%; adoption is not confirmed.

HR/payroll (one line, as instructed): EPF, SOCSO and Form E, plus stamp duty on employment contracts (salary above RM3,000), the foreign-worker multi-tier levy, and OSH coordinators for more than 5 employees, are all extra burdens per Samenta. Orbyte already covers HR.

What we can build (preparatory only, no filing): a per-business compliance calendar (SSM anniversary, financial year end, SST bi-monthly, licence expiry, stamp-duty 30-day clock); document vaults (typhoid and training proof per staff member, licence copies, signed agreements for 7 years); e-invoice readiness (annual threshold and group test check, buyer TIN capture, flagging transactions above RM10k, month-end consolidation pack within 7 days); and an 'exempt supplier pack' to send to large customers.
